185	- In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14): "in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of November as you get closer to the postseason ... That's when players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)** He did not say whether the postseason gets a distinct taper.
186	- The in-season game week: Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)**
187	- Bye weeks: three practice days, extra rest and recovery, slightly higher practice volume than a game week, a speed and strength top-up, and harder work for players with few game snaps. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q17): "guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)**
188	- The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.16]
189	
190	## Data, technology and reporting
191	
192	- The full technology stack: Catapult (GPS), Kitman Labs (central AMS/data store), Perch (camera-based velocity-based training), Polar (heart rate), and the VALD suite — DynaMo, ForceDecks, ForceFrame, Hub, NordBord, SmartSpeed. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
193	- Kitman Labs is positioned specifically as the cross-technology data store and analysis/visualization layer, distinct from each vendor's own reporting tool (e.g., VALD Hub, OpenField Cloud). **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
194	- System of record: each source system holds its own data (force data in VALD, Catapult data in OpenField), Kitman AMS aggregates, and the source system wins when Kitman disagrees. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q11): "They're separate entities; one doesn't overrule the other. If Kitman had wrong numbers from VALD or OpenField, we would go to those sources to correct it: the source systems overrule any errors Kitman made bringing data into the platform." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q11)**
195	- Documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting) except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]
196	- Credential/login management is currently placeholder-only in the Playbook; a secure credential-vault protocol is named as needed but not yet implemented. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.8; performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
197	- Standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist; building them is named as unfinished Phase 2 work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2] Who builds reports today: strength staff for most teams (interview 2026-09-28, Q28; see Department model).
198	- Tensiomyography (TMG) is part of the toolkit, with a documented setup/operations SOP, but that SOP is headed with the names of a prior Director and Associate Director of Applied Performance (Althoff, Nelson), not Eric, and current active use is unclear from this corpus. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q29)**; was Inferred (legacy document, status unclear) [technologytemplatesop.md] Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q29): "Only Chris Ruf with Track still uses it."
199	
200	## Education and staff development
201	
202	- HHPR 5355 ("Power, Speed, Agility, & Periodization in Training") is Eric's own graduate-level course, co-taught with Chris Ruf and Michael Wenger; grading is split across two exams (10% and 20%), a group training-plan project (20%), and lecture/lab participation (40%), with a practical (teach-back) component on exams. **Inferred (transcript, syllabus content)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.1]
203	- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson model to Baylor's own technology stack (ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar) and to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5] Status: a proposal only. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q30): "It has not been built yet." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q30)**
204	- Curriculum design principle: interns need both the "why" (conceptual education) and the "how" (hands-on technical training) each week, and should leave the program with a professional portfolio of real work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics), not just device-operation checklists. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1, 5.4]
205	- The proposed curriculum deliberately adds sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services, reflecting Baylor's specific department structure (Applied Performance inside Health & Wellness) rather than copying Clemson's Olympic-sports-only framing. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3]
206	
207	---
208	
209	## No material found
210	
211	None. Every one of the sixteen required sections had at least some material. Several sections are thin, though, and should be read as gaps rather than settled positions: **Rehab and return to play**, **Injury risk and prevention**, **Recovery and sleep**, **Nutrition and body composition**, and **Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach**. See `interview-prep.md`.
212	
213	Update after the interview (2026-09-28): four of the five thin sections now have an answer, and for three of them the answer is that nothing formal exists, which is itself the finding. Injury risk: no formal model, ACWR distrusted, screens not acted on (Q12). Recovery and sleep: load design only, nothing objective tracked (Q23). Nutrition: no proactive data flow (Q24). Rehab and RTP: role stated (Q4, Q22) and a written protocol exists in the UE and LE templates (Q4a), not yet staged. Coaching stays thin: constraints-led coaching is not used (Q25), and the rest is unclaimed course material.
214	
215	---
216	
217	## Tensions and contradictions
218	
219	Status after the interview (2026-09-28): resolved 1 (partly), 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9; still open 7 (partly), 8, 10. New tensions from the interview are 11 to 16. Resolved by Eric 2026-10-02: 12, 16 and 18 (COD/FMS gates). Each entry below carries its status on its last line.
220	
221	1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.
222	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): partly resolved.** Q1 claimed four positions (Vermeil hierarchy, undulating periodization, Dynamic Correspondence, the football energy-system stack), now Explicit. Every other transcript bullet stays Inferred.
223	
224	2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.
225	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q5): "Both." Both framings are true at once.
226	
227	3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.
228	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q6): the coach's eye flags where to look; data then investigates. The two are sequential, not rival defaults.
229	
230	4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.
231	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q8): V12 "is not current"; a new manual built on the NCAA technology and sport-science recommendations is in development. All V12 bullets are marked Legacy.
232	
233	5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.
234	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved by Q8.** Inference: with V12 not current, the Force Plate Testing V3 cues govern. Eric did not address the cueing question itself.
235	
236	6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]
237	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q20): "Age-based." The body-size table is marked Superseded. Note that the body-size table was from Eric's own assigned session, so his slides and his practice differ.
238	
239	7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.
240	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): still open, confirmed.** Eric (Q30): the intern curriculum "has not been built yet."
241	
242	8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.
243	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): open.** Not asked. Inference: the Q3 rule ("if it doesn't answer a question anyone has...") would retire the roster-wide SOP.
244	
245	9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.
246	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric claimed undulating periodization (Q1).
247	
248	10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.
249	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): open.** Not asked.
250	
251	New tensions raised by the interview (2026-09-28):
252	
253	11. **Eric's own slide against his interview on residual effects.** The class-4 slide (p. 47), from a session Eric taught, says aerobic fitness is lost fastest and speed slowest. In the interview he sides with Issurin, speed fades fastest (Q16), and says Issurin drives speed programming. The slide bullet is marked Superseded. Inference: the slide still circulates in HHPR 5355 and should be reconciled before next spring. The peaking synthesis keeps the counter-evidence both ways.
254	12. **Daily mRSI testing against a Wednesday read.** The SportSmith piece describes mRSI from daily CMJ testing as the daily readiness marker [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]. Q2 names Wednesday as the day. Inference: daily collection with one weekly decision day would reconcile them, but Eric did not say which; worth one follow-up.
255	    **Status: RESOLVED 2026-10-02 (Eric).** Daily jumps are collected to build the rolling baseline and SWC; Wednesday is the single decision read that changes the week.
256	13. **"We don't assess readiness" against mRSI as the readiness marker.** Q22 says Applied Performance does not assess readiness in RTP; the SportSmith piece and Q2 describe mRSI readiness reads. Inference: Q22 is scoped to RTP, so these probably do not conflict, but the RTP templates should be checked.
257	14. **"Support" role against "it doesn't really end".** The Playbook frames RTP input as support to Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance decisions [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]. Q4 describes ongoing testing, progression and shared loading decisions with no end point. Inference: compatible (support can be continuous), but the Playbook wording understates the role.
258	15. **The Q3 rule against current practice.** Eric's rule is that a test with no question or need has no place (Q3). Yet ACWR is still looked at ("We dabble with ACWR") though he does not "trust it for anything", and movement screens are "just collected" without changing decisions (Q12). Inference: by his own rule both are candidates to retire or to be given a question.
259	16. **No true 1RM against %1RM prescription.** No sport tests true 1RM (Q10), while Prilepin's chart and the phase bands are written in %1RM [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]. Inference: loads are percentages of projected maxes, so their error carries into every prescription. Not a contradiction in practice, but worth stating.
260	    **Status: RESOLVED 2026-10-02 (Eric).** Keep %1RM and Prilepin prescription, stated explicitly as built on projected maxes (observation plus history, Q10), not tested 1RMs.
261	17. **DSI as a plyo-vs-strength switch against the evidence.** Eric uses DSI to choose plyometric versus max-strength emphasis (Q21). The evidence check (`docs/synthesis/_work/dsi-evidence-check.md`) finds that IMTP PF explains most of DSI's variance, that the 0.60/0.80 cutoffs were never validated, and that the one controlled trial found a benefit only in its strength arm. Inference: keep the test, but decide on CMJ PF and IMTP PF alongside the ratio, and set cutoffs from the roster.
262	18. **COD and FMS gates in the RTP templates against Q12/Q13.** The LE template gates Evaluation on the 10-5 COD test and on FMS > 14 (`docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`), while Q13 says COD is not tested in most sports and Q12 says screens do not change decisions.
263	    **Status: RESOLVED 2026-10-02 (Eric).** The gates stay in the RTP templates. The baseline names who runs them (Athletic Medicine or the sport coach), not Applied Performance, consistent with "the template answers readiness" (Q22).
264	
265	---
266	
267	## Named influences

269	| Influence | What's credited to them | Where | Provenance |

271	| Al Vermeil (transcribed once as "Albert Meal") | Hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity → strength → power → speed → sport skill); described as the department's programming "compass" | class1-transcript.md pp.9-10, 18-19 | Claimed by Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q1) |

# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)

Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26. Revised 2026-09-28 with Eric's method interview (`docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`, 30 of 30 answered).

## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)

Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:

- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.

Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).

Tags added 2026-09-28 from the method interview:

- **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric stated or claimed the position in the interview. His words are quoted as "Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Qn):". Q1 claimed exactly four course positions (Vermeil hierarchy, undulating periodization, Dynamic Correspondence, the football energy-system priority stack); other course material stays Inferred.
- **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric said the source or practice is not current. The old content is kept and marked, not deleted, so a synthesis note can see what changed.
- **Superseded by interview (Qn)**: a documented position, sometimes from Eric's own slides, that his interview answer replaces.

---

## Philosophy and decision principles

- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]
- Data collection is judged on cost versus insight: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally: "The lesson wasn't about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful ... even a valid test stops being valuable" without staff ownership and consistent collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- General rule for any test or technology, stated as a standing rule rather than a fresh call each time. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)**
- The coach's eye and objective data work in sequence: the eye flags, data investigates. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q6)**
- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- Reject ownership language ("my team," "my athletes"): the athlete's development is shared across every department that touches them, not owned by any one coach. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5, "we got to get away from like the me and my"]
- Attribution in practice: outside frameworks are absorbed into the team's own way of working rather than credited to one person. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q27): "We fold it into the mantra of 'this is how we do our business.'" **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q27)** Inference: this is how Eric applies the "we/our" bullet above, so that bullet reads as practice, though the transcript line itself is still unclaimed.
- The "five expectations" culture rules (Golden Rule, Be Disciplined, Be Relentless, Communicate, No Excuses) were presented in the course as absolute [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.1-2]. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q26): "These are more a relic of another coaching era that has held over. ## Conditioning and energy systems

- Conditioning is defined two ways: (1) how well an athlete can meet the energy requirements of their specific sport/activity, and (2) how well they sustain strength, speed, and power output across a full competition. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.22]
- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]; claimed again in the interview, **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**
- Glycolytic conditioning is still not a primary target in season, but staff do program it in the off-season. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q19): "It does hold up, but our staff does program it in the off-season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)**
- Anaerobic (lactate) threshold heart-rate zones are assigned by athlete body size rather than a single number: roughly 165 bpm for big/tall athletes, 170 for medium, 175 for small, with Zone 1-4 bands set as percentages of that individual threshold. **Superseded by interview (Q20)**; was Explicit [class-4-2026.md pp.28-29]
- The anaerobic-threshold heart rate in use is the age-based method (the slide deck's max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at about 85% of that [class-4-2026.md p.27]). Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q20): "Age-based." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q20)** Resolves Tension 6.
- The traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest; this ordering is used to sequence what needs the most frequent re-exposure. **Superseded by interview (Q16)**; was Explicit [class-4-2026.md p.47] Eric now sides with Issurin (speed fades fastest). See Tension 11.
- Training intensities between roughly 75-90% of maximal effort are labeled (via Francis) "no man's land" — too fast to build alactic power cleanly, too slow to build real aerobic capacity — and are treated as a zone to generally avoid as a primary training target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.48]
- "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
- For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
- Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
- Joel Jamieson's *Ultimate MMA Conditioning* is recommended as the single best practical resource for energy-system development, on the basis that its methods transfer cleanly to non-combat sports despite the MMA framing. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md pp.49-50; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]

## Injury risk and prevention

- Bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk in its own right: an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
- No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; the detailed treatment of ACWR and injury-risk modeling that does exist (Clemson curriculum) is reference material only, not confirmed Baylor practice. Confirmed by the interview: there is no formal risk model.
- ACWR is looked at but not trusted for any decision. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12): "We dabble with ACWR but I don't personally trust it for anything. I think it's raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally. We don't have any formal risk model that we follow. We've avoided them up to this point, but there's not a really good reason why." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q12)**
- Movement screens are collected and filed, not used to change programs. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12): "there isn't anything that changes decisions made to a program; it's more or less just collected and referred to for future needs." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q12)** Inference: this sits uneasily with his own Q3 rule; see Tension 15.

*Thin discipline, now answered: the finding is that nothing formal exists (no risk model, ACWR distrusted, screens not acted on).*

## Nutrition and body composition

- Performance Nutrition is explicitly a separate Health & Wellness unit from Applied Performance, owning individual nutrition consultations, supplement education, body composition and bone density assessment, and the training table/fueling stations. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.5]
- Body composition testing is capped at no more than 4 times per year. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Anthropometrics"]
- Anthropometrics (height, weight, muscle-to-fat ratio) are described as strongly associated with success in most sports and worth tracking even though they are owned by Performance Nutrition rather than Applied Performance. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Anthropometrics"]
- No nutrition decision rules, body-composition targets, or thresholds are attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; this appears to be a deliberate department-design choice (Performance Nutrition owns it) rather than an oversight.
- No force-plate or GPS data flows to Performance Nutrition; bodyweight is consulted only when there is a problem. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q24): "It does not. Only if there is an issue will bodyweight be consulted. Nothing proactive." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q24)**

*Thin discipline, now answered: the finding is that there is no proactive data link between Applied Performance and Performance Nutrition.*

## Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach

- A trained "coach's eye," built through repetition and attention, is treated as at least as important as any technology for daily assessment: "you don't need a fancy test or anything to do that. But you do have to have a good coach's eye." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.8] Eric's own position (interview 2026-09-28, Q6) is narrower: the eye tells you where to look, and data then investigates. See the Philosophy bullet and Tension 3.
- Constraints-led and external-cue coaching are not part of Eric's practice. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q25): "I don't apply it, as I don't fully understand it. I want to know more." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q25)** A learning request, a candidate for a primer.
- New movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3-4 weeks of practice to become efficient and low-energy-cost, which informs how much proficiency to expect when a new exercise or drill is introduced. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.6-7]
- Movement efficiency (skill) is treated as directly reducing energy cost — elite athletes (cited examples: LeBron James, Deion Sanders) are described as outlasting and outperforming peers partly through tactical efficiency that lowers the physical output required to achieve the same result. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.8-9]
- Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced, on the observed premise that many incoming athletes have high sport-specific skill from early specialization but poor general movement competency. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]

*Still thin. The interview added the coach's-eye rule (Q6) and confirmed that constraints-led coaching is not in use (Q25). The rest of this section is shared course material, unclaimed.*

## Periodization and programming

- Macro/meso/microcycle structure is used as the standard planning language, with an explicit reminder that a "training week" does not have to equal 7 calendar days — it can be extended to fit training themes around a real competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.17-18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
- The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume), before a transition into competition. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]
- In-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity even when the practice schedule looks repetitive week to week, specifically to avoid training monotony for the athlete. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21]
- Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block — "you can't ride two horses with one saddle." Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29; week1-lecture.md p.70]
- An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract: lay out the competition calendar, key non-training dates (holidays, exam weeks), and phase-by-phase volume/intensity waves, then adapt the route as circumstances change while still reaching the same destination. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.22-23; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.13-15]
- Training residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue readiness for max-velocity work degrades. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27] Inference: these are Issurin's figures, and Eric sides with Issurin (interview 2026-09-28, Q16), so the speed half reads as his; the aerobic and strength halves were not asked directly.
- In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14): "in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of November as you get closer to the postseason ... That's when players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)** He did not say whether the postseason gets a distinct taper.
- The in-season game week: Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)**
- Bye weeks: three practice days, extra rest and recovery, slightly higher practice volume than a game week, a speed and strength top-up, and harder work for players with few game snaps. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q17): "guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)**
- The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.16]

## Data, technology and reporting

- The full technology stack: Catapult (GPS), Kitman Labs (central AMS/data store), Perch (camera-based velocity-based training), Polar (heart rate), and the VALD suite — DynaMo, ForceDecks, ForceFrame, Hub, NordBord, SmartSpeed. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Kitman Labs is positioned specifically as the cross-technology data store and analysis/visualization layer, distinct from each vendor's own reporting tool (e.g., VALD Hub, OpenField Cloud). **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- System of record: each source system holds its own data (force data in VALD, Catapult data in OpenField), Kitman AMS aggregates, and the source system wins when Kitman disagrees. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q11): "They're separate entities; one doesn't overrule the other. If Kitman had wrong numbers from VALD or OpenField, we would go to those sources to correct it: the source systems overrule any errors Kitman made bringing data into the platform." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q11)**
- Documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting) except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]
- Credential/login management is currently placeholder-only in the Playbook; a secure credential-vault protocol is named as needed but not yet implemented. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.8; performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
- Standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist; building them is named as unfinished Phase 2 work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2] Who builds reports today: strength staff for most teams (interview 2026-09-28, Q28; see Department model).
- Tensiomyography (TMG) is part of the toolkit, with a documented setup/operations SOP, but that SOP is headed with the names of a prior Director and Associate Director of Applied Performance (Althoff, Nelson), not Eric, and current active use is unclear from this corpus. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q29)**; was Inferred (legacy document, status unclear) [technologytemplatesop.md] Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q29): "Only Chris Ruf with Track still uses it."

## Education and staff development

- HHPR 5355 ("Power, Speed, Agility, & Periodization in Training") is Eric's own graduate-level course, co-taught with Chris Ruf and Michael Wenger; grading is split across two exams (10% and 20%), a group training-plan project (20%), and lecture/lab participation (40%), with a practical (teach-back) component on exams. **Inferred (transcript, syllabus content)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.1]
- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson model to Baylor's own technology stack (ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar) and to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5] Status: a proposal only. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q30): "It has not been built yet." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q30)**
- Curriculum design principle: interns need both the "why" (conceptual education) and the "how" (hands-on technical training) each week, and should leave the program with a professional portfolio of real work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics), not just device-operation checklists. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1, 5.4]
- The proposed curriculum deliberately adds sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services, reflecting Baylor's specific department structure (Applied Performance inside Health & Wellness) rather than copying Clemson's Olympic-sports-only framing. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3]

---

## No material found

None. Every one of the sixteen required sections had at least some material. Several sections are thin, though, and should be read as gaps rather than settled positions: **Rehab and return to play**, **Injury risk and prevention**, **Recovery and sleep**, **Nutrition and body composition**, and **Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach**. See `interview-prep.md`.

Update after the interview (2026-09-28): four of the five thin sections now have an answer, and for three of them the answer is that nothing formal exists, which is itself the finding. Injury risk: no formal model, ACWR distrusted, screens not acted on (Q12). Recovery and sleep: load design only, nothing objective tracked (Q23). Nutrition: no proactive data flow (Q24). Rehab and RTP: role stated (Q4, Q22) and a written protocol exists in the UE and LE templates (Q4a), not yet staged. Coaching stays thin: constraints-led coaching is not used (Q25), and the rest is unclaimed course material.

---

## Tensions and contradictions

Status after the interview (2026-09-28): resolved 1 (partly), 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9; still open 7 (partly), 8, 10. New tensions from the interview are 11 to 16. Resolved by Eric 2026-10-02: 12, 16 and 18 (COD/FMS gates). Each entry below carries its status on its last line.

1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.
   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): partly resolved.** Q1 claimed four positions (Vermeil hierarchy, undulating periodization, Dynamic Correspondence, the football energy-system stack), now Explicit. Every other transcript bullet stays Inferred.

2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.
   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q5): "Both." Both framings are true at once.

3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.
   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q6): the coach's eye flags where to look; data then investigates. The two are sequential, not rival defaults.

4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.
   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q8): V12 "is not current"; a new manual built on the NCAA technology and sport-science recommendations is in development. All V12 bullets are marked Legacy.

5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.
   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved by Q8.** Inference: with V12 not current, the Force Plate Testing V3 cues govern. Eric did not address the cueing question itself.

6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]
   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q20): "Age-based." The body-size table is marked Superseded. Note that the body-size table was from Eric's own assigned session, so his slides and his practice differ.

7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.
   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): still open, confirmed.** Eric (Q30): the intern curriculum "has not been built yet."

8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.
   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): open.** Not asked. Inference: the Q3 rule ("if it doesn't answer a question anyone has...") would retire the roster-wide SOP.

9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.
   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric claimed undulating periodization (Q1).

10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.
   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): open.** Not asked.

New tensions raised by the interview (2026-09-28):

11. **Eric's own slide against his interview on residual effects.** The class-4 slide (p. 47), from a session Eric taught, says aerobic fitness is lost fastest and speed slowest. In the interview he sides with Issurin, speed fades fastest (Q16), and says Issurin drives speed programming. The slide bullet is marked Superseded. Inference: the slide still circulates in HHPR 5355 and should be reconciled before next spring. The peaking synthesis keeps the counter-evidence both ways.
12. **Daily mRSI testing against a Wednesday read.** The SportSmith piece describes mRSI from daily CMJ testing as the daily readiness marker [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]. Q2 names Wednesday as the day. Inference: daily collection with one weekly decision day would reconcile them, but Eric did not say which; worth one follow-up.
    **Status: RESOLVED 2026-10-02 (Eric).** Daily jumps are collected to build the rolling baseline and SWC; Wednesday is the single decision read that changes the week.
13. **"We don't assess readiness" against mRSI as the readiness marker.** Q22 says Applied Performance does not assess readiness in RTP; the SportSmith piece and Q2 describe mRSI readiness reads. Inference: Q22 is scoped to RTP, so these probably do not conflict, but the RTP templates should be checked.
14. **"Support" role against "it doesn't really end".** The Playbook frames RTP input as support to Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance decisions [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]. Q4 describes ongoing testing, progression and shared loading decisions with no end point. Inference: compatible (support can be continuous), but the Playbook wording understates the role.
15. **The Q3 rule against current practice.** Eric's rule is that a test with no question or need has no place (Q3). Yet ACWR is still looked at ("We dabble with ACWR") though he does not "trust it for anything", and movement screens are "just collected" without changing decisions (Q12). Inference: by his own rule both are candidates to retire or to be given a question.
16. **No true 1RM against %1RM prescription.** No sport tests true 1RM (Q10), while Prilepin's chart and the phase bands are written in %1RM [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]. Inference: loads are percentages of projected maxes, so their error carries into every prescription. Not a contradiction in practice, but worth stating.
    **Status: RESOLVED 2026-10-02 (Eric).** Keep %1RM and Prilepin prescription, stated explicitly as built on projected maxes (observation plus history, Q10), not tested 1RMs.
17. **DSI as a plyo-vs-strength switch against the evidence.** Eric uses DSI to choose plyometric versus max-strength emphasis (Q21). The evidence check (`docs/synthesis/_work/dsi-evidence-check.md`) finds that IMTP PF explains most of DSI's variance, that the 0.60/0.80 cutoffs were never validated, and that the one controlled trial found a benefit only in its strength arm. Inference: keep the test, but decide on CMJ PF and IMTP PF alongside the ratio, and set cutoffs from the roster.
18. **COD and FMS gates in the RTP templates against Q12/Q13.** The LE template gates Evaluation on the 10-5 COD test and on FMS > 14 (`docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`), while Q13 says COD is not tested in most sports and Q12 says screens do not change decisions.
    **Status: RESOLVED 2026-10-02 (Eric).** The gates stay in the RTP templates. The baseline names who runs them (Athletic Medicine or the sport coach), not Applied Performance, consistent with "the template answers readiness" (Q22).

---

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

# Review: Supertraining Ch 5c (sections 5.3-5.6), 26 entries

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent, instructed to falsify). Date: 2026-10-03.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, PDF idx 298-323 (printed 287-312), plus PDF 91, 375, 381, 536.
Pages opened as images by the reviewer (renders in `staging/_renders/r5c_p*.png`): 298, 300 (plus a 300 dpi crop of Fig 5.12), 301, 302, 303, 304, 305, 306, 307, 308, 309, 310, 312, 313, 314, 315, 316, 317, 318, 319, 320, 321, 322, 323, 375. Pages 381 and 536 were read from the text layer only (clean text, no figures or tables used from them). PDF 91 was checked in the text layer for the Ch1 quote.
Also checked: every "Eric's baseline:" quote against `docs/method-baseline.md` (lines 32, 61, 76, 102, 103, 104, 105, 107, 115, 119, 122, 123, 124, 129, 142, 151, 173, 182, 183, 184 and Tension 17 at line 261; all quotes and evidence tags match); all 74 wikilinks resolve in the vault or staging; the Issurin 2016 vault brief; the Issurin 2008 entries; the Bompa vault entries; the Bondarchuk transfer-ceiling entry; and Bompa & Haff 5e itself (Drive copy, PDF idx 61) for the Bompa finding.

## Entry table

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| case-study--deniskin-depth-jumps-after-resistance-and-rest-as-a-training-means.md | FIX | Fig 5.14 reading is incomplete. Entry: "Ss and Se both rise through stages 1-3, and Ss falls back from its stage-3 high at the stage-4 test." Image (PDF 301 / p.290): within stage 3 both curves fall (Ss about 700 to about 650; Se about 430 to about 375), and at the stage-4 test Se (about 390) is also below its stage-3 start, not only Ss. The rises happen across the rest weeks (8 and 16), which is the text's point. Everything else checked: stage layout weeks 1-7 / 8 / 9-15 / 16 / 17-21 / 22 / 23-24, Fmax about 103 to 110 to about 125 kgf, tmax about 0.42 to about 0.27 s, all quotes, "complete rest" wording, Deniskin 1976. | Replace the last sentence of the figure description with: "Ss and Se jump after each rest week (weeks 8 and 16) and are highest at the start of stage 3; both then decline through stage 3 and sit below that peak at the stage-4 test (Ss about 600-620, Se about 390). Values read by eye from the image." |
| case-study--junior-sprinters-short-and-long-jump-training-effects.md | FIX | Bar values misread. From a 300 dpi crop of Fig 5.12 (PDF 300 / p.289; left axis 0-0.5 s, right panel 0-1.0 s), short / long / combined: 30 m LS about 0.39 / 0.08 / 0.24-0.25 (entry: 0.29 combined); 30 m SS about 0.08 / 0.14 / 0.19 (entry 0.07 / 0.13 / 0.20, fine); 60 m LS about 0.27 / 0.20 / 0.29 (entry 0.29 / 0.22 / 0.33); 60 m SS about 0.07 / 0.38 / 0.42 (fine); 100 m LS about 0.29 / 0.48 / 1.0 (entry 0.27 / 0.50 / 1.0, close). With the corrected values, combined is below the sum at 30 m SS (0.19 vs 0.22), 60 m LS (0.29 vs 0.47) and roughly equal at 60 m SS (0.42 vs 0.45); only 100 m exceeds the sum. The contested reading itself holds and is stronger: short beats combined at 30 m LS by about 0.15 s. Note also an unexplained white outlined bar at the right edge of the 100 m panel reaching 1.0 (may be the frame); treat as unclear. Quotes, "eight months", group definitions checked. | Replace the bar-height sentence with: "30 m LS about 0.39 / 0.08 / 0.25 s; 30 m SS about 0.08 / 0.14 / 0.19 s; 60 m LS about 0.27 / 0.20 / 0.29 s; 60 m SS about 0.07 / 0.38 / 0.42 s; 100 m LS about 0.29 / 0.48 / 1.0 s. An outlined bar at the right edge of the 100 m panel also reaches 1.0; it may be part of the frame and is unclear." In When NOT to apply replace the comparison sentences with: "the short-jump group, not the combined group, shows the largest drop at 30 m LS (about 0.39 vs 0.25 s). Against the sum of the two single groups, the combined bar is below it at 30 m SS (0.19 vs 0.22) and 60 m LS (0.29 vs 0.47), about equal at 60 m SS (0.42 vs 0.45), and above it only at 100 m LS (1.0 vs 0.77)." Update the Example to "about 0.29 s for short jumps alone and about 0.48 s for long jumps alone". |
| case-study--novice-strength-and-speed-strength-sequencing-experiments.md | FIX | One of the three "contested" strands is a misreading. Entry: p.300's "slightly smaller effect" for mixed sessions vs p.299's "A relatively larger effect" is called a contradiction. It is not: p.299's comparator is "the above-mentioned variants" (strength-first vs speed-strength-first across the preparatory period); p.300's comparator is the best variant, the Fig 5.13 complexes. Mixed > order variants and best > mixed are compatible. The other two strands are real and on the cited pages: p.300 ranks strength-then-speed-strength in one session "Least effective" while p.299 found "no statistically significant difference"; p.299 says order "has no real significance for novices" while experiment 3 on the same page favours weights then depth jumps. Also missing: p.299 defines the mixed regime as separate sessions "with a rest interval between sessions on the same day." Names checked against the image (Purvin, Khodykin, Deniskin, Tatian, Chernousov). Baseline line 173 checked. | Delete the sentence beginning "The first sentence ranks mixed sessions below the best variant, while PDF p. 299 says mixed sessions gave 'A relatively larger effect';" and keep the two real strands. Add: "The book also states, in 5.2.4, that resistance plus plyometrics works best 'provided the resistance movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions' (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277), which sits against experiment 4's null within-session result in novices." In item 2 add: "(the mixed regime used separate sessions 'with a rest interval between sessions on the same day', PDF p. 299)." Add `[[claim--depth-jump-training-beat-higher-volume-traditional-training-in-jumpers]]` to Related. |

Entry: "Inference: the authors' warning is about volume, not intensity, which fits that rule." PDF 302 / p.291 also blames intensity: Filinov, "excessively heavy strength loads diminish the force and speed of boxers' punches," and "excessive maximum strength training can impair speed-strength and technical skill." Everything else checked against the image: 30% "as much as", Kotz, Filinov, Deniskin 1976, 18 weeks (54 workouts), 50-60 sessions / about 12 weeks, "rubber-stamp", Siff attribution for the Verkhoshansky-naming passage (correct). | Replace the inference with: "Inference: the authors' warning covers both prolonged high volume (Deniskin) and excessive heaviness (Filinov; 'excessive maximum strength training'), so it supports the in-season 'reduce volume' half of that rule but does not by itself endorse holding heavy intensity during specialised speed phases." |

Entry: "10-15 repetitions at over 80% of 1RM is not possible for most lifters; treat that number as unclear." The image (PDF 313 / p.302) confirms the book's wording; the impossibility claim is the writer's. All quotes checked against PDF 312 / p.301 and 313 / p.302 images: "a moderate compromise", Morgan and Adamson 1953 Leeds (PDF 311 text), "It has been shown", "A literature review reveals", alternation on separate days superior, "This is not to state that circuit training is of little value". Baseline line 115 checked. | Replace with: "Inference: 10-15 repetitions at over 80% of 1RM is beyond most lifters' capacity, so treat that figure as doubtful even though the image confirms the wording." |
| framework--aerobic-vs-anaerobic-circuit-parameters.md | FIX | Contested is overstated in one strand. The PDF 317 / p.306 scheme is explicitly "applicable to the average programme designed to moderately enhance muscle endurance and cardiovascular performance," a different target from the anaerobic column, so it is not a third figure for the same quantity. The real clash is within one category: anaerobic circuits defined as 3-8 reps at over 70% 1RM, then the anaerobic muscle-endurance sub-case at about 50% 1RM and about 50 reps (image confirms "50"). Every table value checked against the image, PDF 315 / p.304: 20-40, 30%, 5-10, 1-4 min, 3-8, 3-5, 70%, 50% / 50 / 4, 75% / 5 / 2 min / 3, 20-30 s. PDF 316 agility/restoration and PDF 317 40-50% of 10RM/5RM/1RM and 80% checked. Baseline line 124 checked. | Replace the contested paragraph opening with: "**Contested inside the book (muscle-endurance figures).** The anaerobic column says 3-8 reps at over 70% of 1RM, but the muscle-endurance sub-case of the same anaerobic category says about 50% of 1RM for about 50 reps (the image confirms '50'), which falls outside both columns. The 40-50% of 10RM, 5RM or 1RM scheme on PDF p. 317 is for a different target ('moderately enhance muscle endurance and cardiovascular performance') and is a separate prescription, not a contradiction." Keep the rest. |
| framework--circuit-layout-variants-superset-retrophase-zigzag-detour.md | FIX | Unlabelled application in When to apply: "The superset equivalence is useful when writing programmes: a two-exercise superset can be planned and progressed with the same rules as a circuit." The book only states the equivalence (PDF 320 / p.309, Fig 5.29). Figures 5.29-5.33 checked against images PDF 320-321; pyramid 40-80% 1RM and 10 to 4 reps, stripping about 10 kg, 60 kg x10 to 100 kg x6 then 90/80/70 kg, spotter quote checked at PDF 322; water resistance quote checked at PDF 317; dripping water at PDF 318. | Prefix: "Inference: the superset equivalence is useful when writing programmes ..." |

`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching` attributes to Siff and Verkhoshansky that gains "may appear **4 to 12 weeks** after the concentrated block ends," and treats 4-12 weeks as the delay to the rebound.
