3	######## PDF 362
4	SUPERTRAINING
5	It has been noted already that the specifics of adaptation are determined primarily by two factors, namely the 
6	work regime in sports, and the gradual, but steady increase in complexity of the body's external interactions 
7	associated with the growth of sporting proficiency.
8	For example, improvement of the triple jump requires developing the ability of the motor apparatus to 
9	produce great power. Increase in jumping distance, which is accomplished primarily by increasing running 
10	speed, is associated with a significant increase in complexity of the interaction of the feet with the support at each 
11	take-off, a situation that requires significant improvement in reactive ability.
12	Cyclic locomotion, to a great extent, necessitates increasing the power and the capacity of the body's systems 
13	which are crucial for energy production of muscular work. Energy expenditure increases greatly with increase in 
14	movement speed. For example, oxygen requirements increase considerably with running speed, energy 
15	expenditure being almost proportional to the fourth power of running speed (Sargent, 1926). This rising cost of 
16	running speed is associated with a greater reliance being placed on anaerobic processes for generating the 
17	necessary energy of work (Henry, 1951; Margaria, 1963).
18	As discussed previously (see 2.2.3, 5.4.3). two forms of functional perfecting of the body may be 
19	distinguished in the training process, namely, specialisation by physiological system and specialisation by motor 
20	ability (Verkhoshansky, 1971). The most obvious evidence of specialisation appears when comparing the 
21	functional development of the body in different sports. 
22	If we refer to the classification scheme of 6.5, 
23	specialisation by physiological system means that acyclic sports rely predominantly on anaerobic processes and 
24	functional hypertrophy of the motor apparatus, whereas cyclic sports place major reliance on aerobic processes. 
25	In complex (combined) sports, there is an intense functional development of both the motor apparatus and the 
26	energy production systems. 
27	Specialisation by motor ability refers to the exact programme of neuromuscular 
28	control that is developed by repetitive execution of the motor skills required in a given sport (see 2.2.3).
29	However, it is important to emphasize that specialisation in the first two cases does not imply that 
30	development is either strictly aerobic or anaerobic, but rather that there is a particular primary emphasis of 
31	functional specialisation. One can successfully develop a high level of explosive strength in acyclic locomotion 
32	only when one possesses sufficiently high aerobic efficiency. At the same time, improving the efficiency of the 
33	energy producing systems in cyclic locomotion should be based on highly developed muscular strength and local 
34	muscular endurance.
35	The kinesiological patterns of motor activity in various types of sports are approximately equivalent, 
36	although there are some qualitative and quantitative differences associated with specific types of sports. Thus, 
37	sprint swimmers have higher rates and developmental levels of anaerobic productivity than distance swimmers, 
38	whereas aerobic productivity is superior for distance swimmers. This is determined by the emphasis of the 
39	training.
40	In the multi-year training of sprinters, up to Class I-CMS (Class I - Candidate for Master of Sport), the chief 
41	emphasis is on developing general (aerobic) endurance and speed, whereas at MS-MSIC (Master of Sport - 
42	Master of Sport, International Class) level the emphasis is on developing speed (anaerobic) endurance. In the 
43	training of distance athletes of all qualification levels, the chief emphasis is on developing aerobic productivity, 
44	while at the MS-MSIC level, the emphasis is on enhancing anaerobic productivity (Vankov, 1978).
45	In cyclic sports, strength preparedness, mainly in the form of strcngth-endurancc, plays an important role. 
46	Research shows that, with a relatively moderate increase in muscular strength, together with a rise in the athlete's 
47	qualification, the qualities of dynamic strength-endurance and power accelerate the increase in functional strength 
48	(Zhurbinoi, 1978).
49	The process of functional specialisation is characterised by the fact that there is a definite sequence (known 
50	as hcterochronicity, as detailed in 2.2.3) in the development of adaptation. This means that the body adapts to 
51	external influences only when they bccome necessary for the further growth of sporting proficiency, and this 
52	involves only those systems whose functions satisfy all the necessary requirements for enhancing sport specific 
53	fitness.
54	The multi-year functional specialisation of the body is closely connected with its corresponding physical 
55	adaptation. This adaptation leaves traces of the training influences on the body for long periods and serves as the 
56	foundation for its functional perfecting. These traces have been studied extensively in general terms at the level of 
57	muscle tissue, cardiac muscle, skeletal structure, cardiovascular mechanisms and other systems. Further study of 
58	the multi-year characteristics of structural-functional specialisation in particular types of sport is important in 
59	formulating the principles of programming training.
60	351
61	
62	
63	######## PDF 363
64	SUPERTRAINING
65	6.8.3 The Structure of Special Physical Preparedness
66	The above-mentioned characteristics of functional specialisation in multi-year training are associated with 
67	specific adaptive changes in the cardiovascular-respiratory and neuromuscular systems, as well as in the 
68	efficiency of the central nervous mechanisms that regulate their activities. For many years, it was not appreciated 
69	that each type of sport requires not only a distinct type of motor skill, but also a different type of physiological 
70	fitness. Even today, the role and nature of supplementary training is not clearly understood. For example, much 
71	the same sort of resistance training may be prescribed for many different athletes in various sports, simply 
72	because the sports seem to be superficially similar. 
73	It must be realised that supplementary or 'cross' training 
74	cannot simply be used in a very general way in the belief that strength, speed or endurance acquired in one 
75	situation will be of direct benefit to performance in another situation.
76	For example, muscle endurance gained through supplementary running training does not mean that it will 
77	directly improve the performance of a competitive rower or cyclist. Special physical preparedness (SPP) depends 
78	on developing the necessary physiological qualities with the same muscles and neuromuscular mechanisms that 
79	are encountered in the given sport. Therefore, training for special physical preparedness must be based on a 
80	thorough understanding of the different types of specificity discussed in 1.3 and the characteristics of the 
81	interaction between the various organs and the neuromuscular system, which determines the change in special 
82	work capacity.
83	It was also assumed that one could develop each fitness quality separately with some or other form of general 
84	training, then assemble all of them to produce the necessary sport specific fitness from them. The emergence of 
85	specificity from an array of non-specific fitness qualities, however, is not supported by current physiological and 
86	biochemical research, so it is clear that the management of training must take into consideration the effects of 
87	concurrent and sequential training means. Therefore, the problem of programming training was examined from 
88	several different positions in earlier chapters (see especially 3.2.1 regarding speed and quickness, and 4.4 
89	regarding general endurance).
90	6.9 Preparedness and the Training Load
91	The connection between the athlete's fitness state and a given loading regime is the central issue in the theory and 
92	practice of programming training (sec 6.3). It is also the weakest link in the management of training, which 
93	requires the special attention of scientists and coaches. Before examining the practical aspects of the connection 
94	between loading and the athlete's fitness state, the concepts of training load and training effect must be defined 
95	more thoroughly (see Fig 6.12).
96	Strictly speaking, the training load does not exist as an independent entity. Terminologically, it must be 
97	distinguished from the load used in weight training, which refers to the resistance or force imposed on the body 
98	by a weight or machinc. Training load is related to the muscular work which the body must produce to carry out 
99	a given regime of exercise in training or competition. More precisely, muscular work is that training potential 
100	which elicits an appropriate training effect from the body. Thus, the training potential of muscular work, and 
101	consequently its training effect is to a large extent determined by the athlete’s current fitness state.
102	It should be clear that the interrelation between the athlete's fitness state and the training load is extremely 
103	complex, dependent upon many factors and determined by numerous variables (see Fig 6.12). Unfortunately, 
104	research concerning this connection is limited and often contradictory. 
105	Therefore, this chapter attempts to 
106	systematise and examine the connection between the athlete's fitness state and the training load, drawing largely 
107	upon the results of extensive research by Verkhoshansky and his co-workers.
108	6.9.1 The Training Load and its Effect
109	The training load refers to the quantitative calculation of the training work performed. It is customary to 
110	recognise the concepts of external, internal and psychological loading, i.e. the quantity of work done, its effect on 
111	the body and the psychologically perceived effect on the athlete, respectively (Matveyev, 1964; Volkov, 1969; 
112	Ozolin, 1970; Tumanyan, 1974). Volume and intensity are used as the most general characteristics of the training 
113	load, as defined in 6.2.2 (Ozolin, 1949; Matveyev, 1956; Khomenkov, 1970; Nabatnikova, 1972).
114	There are other classifications of the training load based on the motor characteristics of the sport, the power 
115	of muscular work^ the pedagogical tasks of the training, the effect on restoration, the effect on subsequent work, 
116	the interaction of work regimes of different emphasis (e.g. the interaction of primarily strength work and speed-
117	352
118	
119	
120	######## PDF 364
121	SUPERTRAINING
122	strength work) and other criteria (Farfel, 1958; Volkov, 1969, 1974; Zimkin, 1963; Monogarov & Platonov, 
123	1975; Suslov, 1978; Scherrer, 1962, 1969).
124	However, each of these classifications, applied separately, are not quite suitable for resolving the task of the 
125	programming of training. A somewhat different approach is required here, which provides special requirements 
126	for the preliminary assessment of the loading and takes into account the above classification criteria.
127	The concept of loading suggests firstly a physiological measure of the effect of specialised muscular work on 
128	the body, reflected in the form of specific functional reactions. Consequently the necessity arose, in developing 
129	the concepts of external and internal loading, for introducing the concepts of the training potential of the loading 
130	and its training effect to enable one to more precisely describe the relationship between cause and effect (see 6.3, 
131	especially Fig 6.12).
132	The influence of the loading is expressed by its training effect (TE), assessed, first of all, by the magnitude of 
133	the change in the athlete's fitness state. 
134	Research concerning the forms in which the TE occurs is very 
135	contradictory, generally amounting to the following representation of events in the training process (Zatsiorsky, 
136	1964; Volkov, 1966; Matveyev, 1977):
137	Acute TE > Delayed TE > Cumulative TE.
138	The first two forms are associated with the single training session: the acute TE is the body’s current reaction to 
139	the physical loading, while the delayed TE is the alteration in the athlete's state observed some time after the 
140	workout. The cumulative TE is the result of the subsequent accumulation of all the TEs that were elicited during 
141	training.
142	However, the above scheme is one-sided and does not take into account the qualitative changes in the TE 
143	when they are produced by training loads of different primary emphasis (e.g. on strength, speed-strength or 
144	muscle endurance). The fact is that the accumulation of training effects is not simply a summation of separate 
145	effects, but a synergistic whole (i.e. the sum of the parts is greater than the whole).
146	The mechanism of generalised adaptation as a universal quality of a biological system establishing a balance 
147	between its state and external conditions, is determined primarily by the automatic selection of an accommodative 
148	strategy which is most appropriate in that situation. This involves selective response to the training influences of 
149	different primary emphasis and their stable integration into a well-adapted system. 
150	As has already been 
151	mentioned, the cumulative TE itself can have a different quantitative and qualitative expression, depending on 
152	factors including the current state of fitness, the order in which training regimes of different emphasis follow each 
153	other, the after-effects of preceding loading, and the duration of given training means (Verkhoshansky, 1970).
154	For example, it has long been known that the result of a workout depends on the sequence of exercises (e.g. 
155	with primary emphasis on speed, strength or endurance). Considerable research has shown clearly the effect of a 
156	particular sequence of training loads of different emphasis during long-term training on the body, e.g. 'aerobic' 
157	and 'anaerobic' glycolytic loading for developing special endurance (Nabatnikova, 1972; Volkov, 1975; Platonov, 
158	1980) or strength and jumping exercises for explosive strength (Tatyan, 1975; Khodykin, 1976; Chemousov, 
159	1978; Levchenko, 1980).
160	Based on similar research, it has been suggested that a distinction be made between the concepts of partial 
161	TE (the result of the effect of loading of one primary emphasis or means) and cumulative TE (the result of the 
162	generalised effect on the body of loading of different primary emphasis, applied concurrently or sequentially). In 
163	the latter case there are both quantitative and qualitative aspects to the TE. The distinction between these 
164	concepts can best be explained by examples.
165	In one experiment (Fig 6.24), group 1 began by using barbell exercises, followed by depth-jumps (a 
166	plyometric method of developing explosive strength). Group 2 used the reverse sequence of means. Each group 
167	of means were used for three months each. Group 3 used the barbell exercises and the depth-jumps concurrently 
168	throughout both 3-month stages. The overall volume of the loading was equivalent in all groups.
169	The results of the studies enabled us first of all to compare the partial TE of utilising only barbell exercises 
170	and depth-jumps (the first stage for groups 1 and 2), as well as the cumulative TE obtained as a result o f two 
171	different ways of organising the loading: concurrent (group 3) and sequential (the second stage of groups 1 and 
172	2). The following conclusions were derived from this experiment:
173	1. The partial TE of the depth-jumping is greater than that of the barbell exercises.
174	353
175	
176	
177	######## PDF 365
178	SUPERTRAINING
179	2. The final effect of the training is altered substantially by re-arrangement of the loading of different primary 
180	emphasis. The sequence of using barbell exercises followed by depth-jumps (group 1) produced a higher 
181	level of speed-strength preparedness (a positive cumulative TE), than the reverse sequence (group 2). Id 
182	group 2 the TE was essentially lower at the end of the second stage than after the first (a negative 
183	cumulative TE).
184	3. The concurrent use of the above means in the first stage (group 3) yielded a larger cumulative effect than in 
185	groups 1 and 2. However, the TE noticeably decreased for group 3 during the second stage because the 
186	lengthy use of a single means decreases the training potential of the loading.
187	Figure 6.24 The training effect of different sequences of speed-strength means for high junipers of medium qualification. Graph I 
188	shows the increase in absolute strength of the plantarflexors; graph 2, the increase in maximal explosive effort in a vertical jump; graph 
189	3, the increase in height after a depth jump. All values in % increase over initial values. White bars = first 3 months; shaded bars = next 
190	3 months of training. (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
191	In another experiment (Fig 6.25), over a 7-week period, group 1 used weights exercises with 30-50% of IRM;

232	6.9.2 Factors determ ining the Training Effect
233	In order to select the optimal training loads from the many possible variations, it is necessary to undertake a 
234	preliminary assessment of their effectiveness. To do this, it is useful to analyse the physical effects of the loading 
235	in terms of characteristics such as its contents, volume and organisation (Fig 6.27). The degree of reliability 
236	providing the effect generated by each of these characteristics has great significance for the success of the 
237	training.

239	We will examine in more detail the basis for a particular selection associated with each characteristic. In doing so, 
240	we will focus our attention on loading intended to develop explosive-strength and specific endurance.

246	The programming of training begins with the determination of its contents, i.e. the composition of the means, 
247	selected on the basis of preliminary assessments using two criteria, namely the specificity of the training load and 
248	the training potential (see Fig 6.27).
249	Specificity of the Load
250	The specificity of the training means refers to their similarity to competition activities regarding motor structure 
251	(including movement patterns), regime of work and mechanism of energy production. This particular criterion is 
252	used to distinguish between means of special and general physical preparedness (SPP and GPP). The SPP means 
253	primarily are for increasing the specific work capacity, whereas the GPP means arc used for general physical 
254	development, for activating restorative processes after prolonged or intense loading, or for facilitating changes 
255	from one type of work to another (Ozolin, 1949; Khomenkov, 1957; Matveyev, 1964).
256	The SPP means should correspond as closely as possible to the dynamics and regime of work of the sports 
257	activity. This requirement is the principle o f dynamic correspondence (discussed in 4.3) which stipulates the 
258	importance of the similarity between the training means and the fundamental sport exercises with respect to the 
259	following indicators (see 4.3):
260	• The amplitude and direction of movement
261	• The accentuated region of force production
262	• The dynamics of the effort (including maximum forcc)
263	• The rate and time of maximum force production
264	• The regime of muscular work.
265	One should, however, take into account that in practice the external similarity of the training means to the 
266	fundamental sport exercise is often overemphasized, whereas the importance of the similarity of the means to the 
267	regime o f muscular work and to the mechanism o f its energy production is underemphasized. It should be noted 
268	that literal similarity of the training means to the fundamental sports activities in motor structure is appropriate 
269	only if it directly improves the athlete's level of physical and technical preparedness (Dyachkov, 1968, 1975).
270	However, for SPP to be effective, it is not so important that the training means precisely mimic the spatial 
271	characteristics of the given exercise. The main criterion of conformity in this case is the regime of muscular work 
272	as a whole. For example, strength exercises such as barbell squats bear little resemblance to the athlete's 
273	movement in running, throwing or playing basketball. However, the use of squats is justified because they 
274	actively contribute to raising the athlete's special work capacity of the appropriate muscles in these sports.
275	An adequate number of SPP means which conform to the fundamental actions is available for training in 
276	every sport. However, it is important to point out that the need to preserve the training potential of the loading 
277	(especially for highly qualified athletes) requires using means that not only conform to, but exceed, competition 
278	conditions, with regard to maximum force, time of maximum force development and the power of the metabolic 
279	processes which determine work-capacity. 
280	On this basis, it is easy to conclude that satisfaction of this 
281	requirement should be associated with improving the strength component of the movement. This emphasis on 
282	strength or, more precisely, the use of specialised strength exercises in the regime of SPP means makes it 
283	necessary to examine this question in more detail.
284	First of all, one must emphasize that the role of strength exercises in sports training is not limited to 
285	enhancing strength alone, as is sometimes thought. It is undoubtedly important to increase strength, but this is 
286	not the fundamental and sole task o f strength training. By itself, the value of maximal strength, in particular, 
287	dwindles and may not sufficiently be utilised in practice for enhancing the effect and specificity of the loading 
288	under actual sporting conditions. However, its role in spced-strength sports is obvious and achieved successfully, 
289	but in many other types of sport (in particular, those requiring endurance), it is still not adequately understood.
290	The development of endurance is associated primarily with using long duration or distance training to 
291	improve aerobic capacity. 
292	However, the importance of muscular adaptation to intense and prolonged work 
293	invariably is underestimated. It also appears to be forgotten that specialisation of the muscles, as the direct 
294	executor of the work, is of greater significance than development of the cardiovascular-respiratory component of 
295	endurance. A more intense stimulus is necessary for promoting adaptation of the muscles to endurance work than 
296	for producing cardiovascular and respiratory conditioning. Therefore, when one uses only the long duration 
297	method for developing endurance, a definite imbalance can arise between the functional level of the

305	This situation is very typical of the preparation of middle-distance runners. Elementary logic decrees that in 
306	order to run 800m in 1:45:0, it is necessary to be able to achieve a time of 10.6-10.7 seconds in the 100m. One 
307	needs to possess great strength potential to do this, e.g. the ability to execute three consecutive standing long 
308	jumps covering a total distance of at least 9m, or ten consecutive standing long jumps totalling 33-34m, for which 
309	middle-distance runners usually do not have the strength. Elimination of this insufficiency is possible only 
310	through specialised strength and jump training which exerts a stronger influence on the muscles than distance 
311	training, thereby intensifying their adaptation to endurance work and activating the relevant functional reserves of 
312	the body. As a result, the power and the capacity of the metabolic processes are enhanced, including ’anaerobic’ 
313	energy production, which provides a high level of local muscular endurance and complements the body's already- 
314	acquired 'aerobic' ability. At the same time, it is possible to reduce the volume of exhausting endurance work in 
315	the 'anaerobic' glycolytic zone (Zhdanovich, 1980; Verkhoshansky & Sirenko, 1982).
316	Methods of executing specialised strength and jumping exercises in endurance sports should firstly increase 
317	strength up to a definite optimum, and secondly, exploit the specific energy processes crucial for producing 
318	repeated motor actions. The characteristics of the sport, practical experience and experimentation should 
319	determine the optimal regimes of specialised strength training in each case. The main thing is to overcome the 
320	archaic viewpoint which regards strength training as a means of increasing absolute strength alone.
321	The GPP means play no less an important role in the organisation of training. Besides improving traditional 
322	multi-faceted motor coordination and creating a foundation for subsequent specialised motor skill training, some 
323	GPP means can activate the restorative processes. This has special significance in those sports in which there are 
324	few supplementary training means and training is inherently monotonous, i.e. where the competition exercises arc 
325	the basic training means (gymnastics, weightlifting and cyclic sports).
326	For example, research showed that the sole and systematic use of swimming restoration procedures during 
327	the execution of voluminous loading produced an increase of 24.2% in absolute strength and 18.9% in strength- 
328	endurancc, whereas swimmers who did not use the restorative procedures increased these indicators by only 7.7% 
329	and 4.9% respectively. At the same time, the volume of the training load was increased by an average of 15% 
330	(Kuchnyev, 1977; Platonov, 1980). 
331	In the pre-competition preparation of highly qualified middle-distance 
332	runners, the complex use of low frequency vibromassage and psycho-regulatory training contributed to an 
333	increase in the speed of training distances by 2-4% and to an increase of 12-20% in training volume, executed at 
334	competition speed (Potapchenko, 1979).
335	Thus, the organised combination of training loads and restorative procedures is an important prerequisite for 
336	intensifying and increasing the effectiveness of training. However, it must be emphasized that restoration after 
337	work is a natural process which occurs in a definite sequence over a certain period. This process occurs through 
338	adaptation of interacting physiological systems to stress generated by systematic loading (Yakovlev, 1971). 
339	Artificially accelerating the restoration process as a routine can disturb the natural course of the body's long-term 
340	adaptation to intense muscular activity and therefore can be justified only in clear cases of over-exertion (Siff & 
341	Yessis, 1992).
342	Frequent and regular application of non-specific means of restoration may hinder the adaptation process, 
343	especially when large training loads are used. Increasing the volume and intensity of the loading disturbs 
344	homeostasis as a basic condition for promoting adaptation to loading and enhancement of the restoration 
345	processes. At the same time, premature intervention during the course of restoration can hinder the body's 
346	supercompensatory ability to enhance this process by natural means (Yevgenyev et al, 1975). The interconnected 
347	process of loading-restoration within the general scheme of sports training should be strictly regulated on the 
348	basis of scientific assessment of the athlete's fitness state.

353	capacity increases; therefore, it is important to preserve it by introducing more effective means into the training.

355	practical possibility of altering the athlete's state by using means with different training potential (A, B, C). 
356	However, it is inappropriate to use highly stimulating means prematurely, because the body is functionally

372	6.9.4 The Volume of the Training Load
373	The volume of the training load refers primarily to the quantitative aspects of training and plays an important role 
374	in the long-term adaptation of the body to intense muscular work.
375	The function of the volume of the load consists chiefly of the systematic and prolonged disturbance of the 
376	body's homeostasis, which stimulates the mobilisation of its energy resources and plastic reserves. This is the 
377	fundamental condition for switching from the acute (specific) reaction provoked by individual components of the 
378	training, to the general (non-specific) adaptive reaction, and then to the development of long-term adaptation of 
379	the body. Therefore, in each successive annual cycle athletes should execute larger volumes o f loading (within 
380	optimal limits) to raise and maintain the special work-capacity.
381	In types of sports requiring brief, highly concentrated efforts, the volume of loading has yet another 
382	important significance. As discussed earlier, the mechanical integrity o f the ligamentous-joint apparatus can 
383	become the limiting factor to the progress o f sporting performance (see 1.6 and 1.7.2). If these connective tissues 
384	are not prepared by extensive work of moderate intensity, then the great dynamic overloading encountered at the 
385	level of peak performance can lead to severe joint injury. This occurs frequently in gymnastics, weightlifting, 
386	high jumping and triple jumping.
387	The volume on its own does not determine the specificity of the training influence of the loading on the body 
388	and the characteristics of the body's adaptive reactions. Therefore, when programming training, the influence of 
389	the volume can be determined correctly only if one also takes into consideration the magnitude of the loading, its 
390	duration and intensity. The magnitude of the volume is the quantitative measure of the actual or planned training 
391	load of a certain primary emphasis calculated during each specific microcycle, stage or annual cycle as a whole 
392	(sec 6.2.2).
393	The magnitude o f the volume is determined, first of all, on the basis of the athlete's qualification. The higher 
394	the qualification, the larger the volume of loading over the year and each stage of preparation. As the athlete's 
395	qualification rises (also within a four-year cycle), so the magnitude, and consequently, the ratio of the loading 
396	volume of different primary emphasis shifts towards an increase in the portion devoted to specialised loading 
397	(Panov, 1975; Zhikharevich, 1976; Vankov, 1977; Matveyev, 1977; Gilyazova, 1978).
398	The magnitude of the annual loading volume is established individually by examining the characteristics of 
399	the athlete's preparation during the preceding stages of training. A more serious task of programming training is 
400	the calculation of the optimal volume of loading in distinct time segments (month, stage or phase). This 
401	magnitude should be determined on the basis of the goals of training during each stage of the annual cycle and 
402	according to the principles of effective organisation of training loads of different primary emphasis, as discussed 
403	in this chapter.

409	The intensity o f the loading determines the strength and specificity of its effect on the body or the difficulty 
410	of the training. The intensity regulates the training potential of the given means, the frequency of their use and 
411	the intervals between repeated means or training sessions with large training potential, as well as the ratio of the 
412	volume of the loading divided by the time taken to reach the maximum load in a given stage. The latter measure 
413	has especially important significance for programming training over prolonged periods, sincc it takes into account 
414	the loading concentration relative to time. Intensification of loading is permitted during specific stages in the 
415	annual cycle and only after preliminary preparation with extensive low intensity loading (see Fig 6.1).
416	The duration o f the training load is a vital measure of the volume and must be discussed in more detail, since 
417	it has a significant effect on the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state and can easily be miscalculated by the 
418	average coach.
419	It has already been mentioned that the length of time over which systematic training regimes are employed 
420	(the general volume of loading) has a definite maximum limit, depending on the current adaptation reserves 
421	(CAR) of the body (see 1.16). At the same time, considerable research has established that there is also an upper 
422	limit to the duration of using any specialised training means with a primary emphasis, the exceeding of which is 
423	detrimental to the development of maximum and explosive strength, as well as to the growth of aerobic and 
424	anaerobic capacity. Exceeding this limit does not enhance fitness and wastes die athlete's time and energy. In 
425	programming training, it is important to determine the optimal duration of loading of any primary emphasis, as 
426	well as a suitable rate of increase of the relevant performance indicators.
427	Unfortunately there is no special research directed at determining the optimal length of time for applying 
428	loading of a specific primary emphasis. However, indirect data has been gathered which sheds some light on this 
429	problem. Thus, there is a linear increase in absolute strength in response to a given regime of loading, which 
430	slows down as the limit of this optimal time-span of training is reached, a point which defines exhaustion of the 
431	body's current adaptation energy (see 1.16). Observation of highly qualified athletes indicates that absolute 
432	strength increases with little variation, rising continuously during the year's training.
433	When explosive strength is the purpose of special training, there is a clear tendency for the rise in explosive 
434	strength to slow down; the sharper its growth, the earlier it plateaus. When one is emphasizing the development 
435	of explosive strength exclusively, the plateau appears within 3-4 months. In those cases where explosive strength 
436	is not the key ability (e.g. in a mono-cycle of periodisation in the annual training of decathletes), the increase in 
437	explosive strength can continue (with some fluctuation) for up to 10 months.
438	Loading that is primarily aerobic will produce significant increases in aerobic efficiency even within one 
439	month of training (Borisov, 1979; Sirenko, 1980). The dynamics of the level of aerobic fitness and the indicators 
440	of aerobic loading executed within the aerobic zone (at a HR of 120-170 beats/minute) parallel one another. 
441	Their rate of increase is approximately the same and is linear over a 2-3 months period. Despite increased loading 
442	volume, the aerobic fitness indicators do not increase significantly later on, but fluctuate around the maximum 
443	level achieved (Zatsiorsky et al, 1974; Skorodymova, 1974; Suslov, 1977; Ustkachkintsev, 1979; Sirenko, 1980).
444	About 4 months are necessary to achieve the highest results in anaerobic-glycolytic productivity (Zatsiorsky 
445	ct al, 1974; Serafimova, 1974; Doroshchenko, 1976; Ustkachkintsev, 1979). Increasing the volume of anaerobic 
446	work produces a positive effect only if it precedes a significant volume of aerobic work, thereby stimulating the 
447	aerobic reaction (Scrafimova, 1974; Naumenko, 1978).
448	Note that the above data applies to the natural conditions of an athlete's preparation, where development of a 
449	given motor ability is achieved together with the execution of other tasks and loading of other primary emphasis. 
450	They conform to those actual loading volumes that highly qualified athletes use according to contemporary 
451	principles of organising training. Since these principles are being constantly refined, the duration of loading 
452	quoted above is not definitive. However, they offer a preliminary guide for the programming of training.
453	6.9.5 The Organisation of Training Loads
454	The organisation of training refers to its regulation over a definite period to ensure attainment of the planned 
455	level of SPP and physical fitness. The basis of such regulation should be the achievement of the positive 
456	cumulative training effect of the loading of different primary emphasis (see Fig 6.26). Here, it is necessary to 
457	observe the chief requirement of maintaining the training potential of the loading. The basic organisational 
458	principles of special strength training, which are discussed in the following sections, are:
459	• The specificity of muscular work

465	• The concentration of loading over time
466	• The separation of strength load, speed development and perfection of technique
467	• Utilisation of the Long-term Training Effect
468	The organisation of loading is defined by two criteria, namely the nature of its distribution over time and the 
469	interrelation between the loads of different primary emphasis.
470	The distribution o f the training load over time refers to the way in which it is organised in separate stages, 
471	cycles and phases of the annual cycle. The distribution of the general volume of loading and its dynamics in the 
472	annual cycle are determined by the traditional periodisation of training and the characteristics of the body's long­
473	term adaptation to training. If one speaks of loading of one primary emphasis, then one must distinguish between 
474	two ways of organising it, namely distributed loading and concentrated loading (see 6.6.1 and Fig 6.23). The first 
475	assumes a relatively uniform distribution of means during an annual cycic; the second, the concentration of 
476	means over definite training stages.
477	The effectiveness of the distribution and concentration methods of organising training loads should be based 
478	on the athlete's level of qualification. Research indicates that both methods arc successful in training athletes of 
479	medium qualification. 
480	The concentrated loading method is appropriate for the training of highly qualified 
481	athletes. In this regard, it has been shown that distribution o f glycolytic work over the annual cycle o f highly 
482	qualified sprinters raises the loading volume, but does not increase the effectiveness o f the loading. However, by 
483	concentrating the volume of glycolytic work at certain stages, the work can be executed at a smaller volume but 
484	with a more significant improvement in speed-endurance (Kornelyuk, 1980). Similar results have been obtained 
485	by concentrating the volume of special strength work of sprinters (Levchenko, 1986), middle-distance runners 
486	(Sirenko & Zhdanovich, 1982), boxers (Filimonov, 1979) and jumpers (Mironenko & Antonova, 1981).
487	The above research has shown that concentration o f the volume o f uni-directional loading produces more 
488	extensive functional changes and greater improvement in the athlete's physical fitness. 
489	The regular use of 
490	training with distributed loading which is dispersed over a prolonged period evokes only a transient functional 
491	reaction which does not enhance the development of long-term adaptation. Distributed loading initially can yield 
492	some rise in functional level but its training potential soon drops because of rapid adaptation of the body to the 
493	training stimuli.
494	The use of loads of different primary emphasis produces the required cumulative training effect, provided 
495	that they arc combined logically over time, since the cumulative loading with means o f different primary 
496	emphasis can have positive or negative effects. Thus, to develop explosive strength, a positive cumulative effect 
497	on the body may be achieved by use of the following brief combinations of training means:
498	• short and long jumping exercises
499	• barbell exercises and jumping exercises
500	• barbell exercises with 30% and 90% of maximum
501	• barbell exercises and the plyomctric method of developing explosivc-strength
502	• leaping with kettle-bells and jumping exercises
503	• barbell exercises and leaping with kettle-bclls.
504	In a single training session the order of the above means, combined in a systematic complex is fairly unimportant, 
505	since the length of time for which the body maintains the after-effect of training stress exceeds the duration of the 
506	workout. During this session and the subsequent restoration period, a generalised summation of the after-effects 
507	of the entire complex of training influences of different primary emphasis occurs, which produces the same 
508	cumulative effect, generally regardless of their sequence. However, it is still sensible to apply the recommended 
509	scheme of Figure 1.7 to minimise the risk of reducing skill and safety.
510	Thus, concerning the development o f explosive strength, the order o f the means is not fundamentally as 
511	important as the volume o f the loading and the degree o f contrast between the different training means. 
512	Nevertheless, one should still preserve the above order of combining means in each case, since this provides the 
513	favourable effect of a brief rise in fitness state, which the first exercise produces as the second one is executed 
514	(see Ch 5.3). The best way of using the above combination of special strength exercises is to employ them 
515	sequentially with active rest between each series. When repeating such a series, it is desirable to vary the exer­
516	cises to avoid monotony and to maintain the optimal rest interval for facilitating recovery.
517	One cannot speak with similar certainty about the effect of the interaction of loading of different primary 
518	emphasis on the development of endurance. Research findings arc inadequate and arc often so contradictory that

532	processes during the short duration activity of strength, strength-speed and strength-endurance sports. Moreover, 
533	no research has analysed the energy processes occurring while the general activity is undoubtedly aerobic, but the 
534	postural muscles are strongly contracted, a situation which suggests that aerobic processes can be strongly active 
535	at a general level while anaerobic processes can also be strongly evident at a local level. This obviously poses a 
536	major problem for the prescription of sport specific training.
537	It is to be hoped that in the near future the negative consequences of such interpretations will be eliminated, 
538	but until then it should be noted that current experimental data indicates that a positive interaction of endurance 
539	loading occurs when:
540	• aerobic exercises are done after ATP-CP training
541	• aerobic exercises are done after glycolytic-anaerobic training (in small volume)
542	• glycolytic-anaerobic exercises are done after ATP-CP training.
543	Under these conditions the previous loading creates favourable conditions for executing the subsequent loading 
544	and raises the effect of the training session as a whole.
545	There is a negative interaction when (Volkov, 1975):
546	• ATP-CP exercises are done after a large amount of any glycolytic work
547	• glycolytic-anaerobic exercises follow large volumes of aerobic work.
548	It has been established that restoration of energy resources and disturbance of endocrinc equilibrium within the 
549	body is prolonged by 2-3 days after a large volume of aerobic work. During this period it is appropriate to 
550	employ a small volume of anacrobic loading which will not negatively influence the restoration of aerobic 
551	capacity and will stimulate the development of anaerobic capacity.
552	Restoration after moderate volumes of anaerobic loading usually takes 3-8 hours. 
553	However, very large 
554	volumes of anaerobic loading will delay restoration. The training effect of ATP-CP workouts deteriorates if the 
555	sessions are done without allowing full restoration from the preceding loading (Nabatnikova, 1972; Volkov, 
556	1975; Platonov, 1980).
557	Sequential accumulation of the training effect of loading of different primary emphasis has a place in long­
558	term preparation and is achieved by the action of preceding work on subsequent work. 
559	In this case, if the 
560	preceding work creates favourable circumstances for the subsequent work, there is a positive accumulation of 
561	their training effects.

563	applies extensive (i.e. high volume) training with submaximal resistance first, followed by explosive training. In

565	potential of the neuromuscular system. This creates favourable conditions for further adaptation, facilitated by the 
566	subsequent loading and emphasis on developing the athlete's ability to display great explosive power. The reverse 
567	sequence of this loading scheme leads to a negative cumulative effect.
568	The mechanism of sequential accumulation is appropriate only if the training effect of the previous work has 
569	become relatively stable, which takes at least 4-6 weeks. When the strength means of different emphasis are

582	• It is permissible and customary to develop explosive abilities with supplementary means that sometimes 
583	deviate far from the motor structure of the fundamental sport exercise; however, the fundamental sport 
584	activity is traditionally the chief means of developing special endurance in cyclic sports. Here the 
585	development of special endurance depends on the optimal selection of the relative volumes of work of 
586	different intensity and duration.
587	• Endurance training causes more profound changes than explosive training within the body and requires more 
588	time for restoration. Therefore, selection o f subsequent training is very important. Sincc it is appropriate to 
589	do work of a different type, which in particular intensifies restoration or improves other abilities, this 
590	complicates the maintenance of the main emphasis of the training regime and leads to use of concurrent 
591	training means, which may not always be appropriate for highly qualified athletes (Platonov, 1980).
592	The methods of developing endurance were established long ago and there are still two opposing viewpoints. One 
593	of these is based on the value of concurrent development of general and special endurance (Matveyev, 1970; 
594	Ogoltsov, 1971; Nabatnikova, 1972). This variant introduces special endurance loading right from the beginning 
595	of the preparatory period, during which one is also developing general endurance. It is assumed that this training 
596	will be more specialised, creating more favourable conditions for specific adaptation to competitive activities. 
597	This point of view has been corroborated experimentally, much of the research having been done with athletes 
598	who had not yet reached the highest levels of sports mastery, in particular with junior middle-distance runners 
599	(Baranov, 1969), swimmers (Kuzovenkov, 1969) and skiers (Malikov, 1974).
600	The viewpoint emphasizes the sequential development of endurance, where one begins by enhancing 
601	cardiovascular capability, followed by anaerobic-glycolytic endurance, and finally, short-term endurance (the 
602	creatine phosphate process). The introduction of aerobic work in this sequence promotes the training-eftect of 
603	anaerobic work (Ozolin, 1959, 1970; Volkov, 1963; Yakovlev, 1957; Borisov, 1979; Loktev, 1978). A gradual 
604	increase in the duration of cardiovascular loading leads to an accumulation of energy substrates and an increase in 
605	the body's energy potential (Yakovlev, ct al, 1960). Here, the intensity of loading, rather than its volume is of 
606	principal significance (Astrand & Rodahl, 1970). When one's cardiovascular ability is insufficient, an excessive 
607	increase in the volume of anaerobic means causes a decrease in sporting performance (Naumenko, 1978; 
608	Vavilov, 1977; Scrafimova, 1974; Morzhevikov, 1980).
609	A third viewpoint on endurance development has been formulated and experimentally verified. Basically, it 
610	involves the increase in volume of concurrent aerobic and anaerobic training means, but with a sequential change 
611	in emphasis from general to special endurance. The effectiveness of this type of training construction in the 
612	annual cycle has been demonstrated, in particular, for highly qualified middle-distance runners (Doroshchenko, 
613	1976; Loktev, 1978; Borisov, 1979), as well as for multi-year training (Linyets, 1979). One can assume that this 
614	system represents a compromise which combines the benefits of concurrent and sequential special endurance 
615	training.
616	The organisation of loading is closely associated with selecting the optimal rest interval between repetitions 
617	in a single training session and between succcssive sessions. It is vital to remember that the essence of training 
618	consists not only of muscular work, but also of the effect of the adaptive reaction elicited by it. Therefore, ihe 
619	rest pause is actually a training means which is just as important as muscular work, so that it should be 
620	employed skillfully. It has been emphasized repeatedly that the art of training management consists of the 
621	systematic combination of specific and non-specific loading, together with careful regulation of work and rest 
622	stages (Hippenreitor, 1955; Petrovsky, 1969; Ozolin, 1949, 1966). The rest interval is one of the most important 
623	components of training methodology. Devising the optimal pause between repetitions and other stages of training 
624	work requires extensive methodological competence and practical skill in utilising this pause effectively.
625	These findings highlight the extremely complex connection between the athlete's state and the training load, 
626	and coupled with this, the difficulty of selecting the optimal method of training organisation to achieve the 
627	desired special work capacity. Nevertheless, despite the paucity of data, which does not allow one to prescribe 
628	exact recommendations for each sport, some principal guidelines for organising annual training loads may be 
629	identified, as given in various sections of this text.
630	6.10 The Long-Term Delayed Training Effect
631	The particular connection between the dynamics of the athlete's state and the loading regime in 
632	long-term 
633	training will now be examined in detail.
634	362
635	
636	
637	######## PDF 374
638	SUPERTRA/N/NG
639	Considerable research (Nikitin, 1977; Mironenko, 1979; Antonova, 1982; Levchenko, 1982) has revealed a 
640	steady decrease in speed-strength preparedness during individual training stages of different length (from 5-12 
641	weeks). This decrease is the result of voluminous strength loading (Figure 6.29, shaded rectangle), after which 
642	speed-strength returns to its initial level and significantly exceeds it. Since this phenomenon does not agree with 
643	established ideas which stipulate a continuous rise in special physical preparedness as an essential condition for 
644	effective organisation of training, and since it is not accompanied by marked signs of overtraining, it has become 
645	a subject of special study. The results of this study occupy the remainder of this section.
646	The volume of the training load has a definite optimum level for each athlete, above or below which the body 
647	reacts with diminished response. There is a characteristically simple connection between the quantity of work and 
648	the dynamics of the athlete’s fitness state.
649	Figure 6.29 The effect of concentrated strength loading on speed-strength indicators of sprinters (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
650	An increase in volume of loading raises the athlete's special work-capacity, whereas a decrease lowers it. If the 
651	volume of loading is lower than the optimum level, special work-capacity decreases after some initial rise. If the 
652	volume of loading significantly exceeds this level, a steady decrease in special work-capacity occurs which, 
653	however, rises intensely during the carefully-timed reduction in the volume. This intense rise in special work- 
654	capacity is the phenomenon known as the long-term delayed training effect (LDTE) which accompanies one of 
655	the forms of adaptation to volume of loading.
656	This phenomenon has been known for some time in practice, where it has been observed as an increase in 
657	performance in several sports after a decrease in the volume of the training load during the pre-competition stage 
658	(Ozolin, 1949, 1967; Dyachkov, 1953; Matveyev, 1970; Charycv, 1975). However, this reflects only the external 
659	evidence of this type of adaptation, and the physiological conditions, mechanisms and characteristics of the 
660	LDTE until recently have not been a subject of much research. Essentially, no one expected that the existence of 
661	the LDTE offered any great promise for systematising training, especially for highly qualified athletes.
662	The LDTE phenomenon of concentrated strength loading has also been observed in several cyclic sports, 
663	including middle-distance running (Zhdanovich, 
664	1980), swimming (Rudokenc, 1981) and ice-skating 
665	(Kabachkova et al, 1982). Thus, a steady increase in the strength-endurance of middle-distance runners was 
666	verified, being reflected in increased stride length and improved results in ten standing long jumps (Fig 6.30) 
667	following a block of concentrated strength loading. It is interesting that there is an increase in the ability of these 
668	runners to produce a single explosive effort (e.g. in vertical jumping) during the concentrated strength loading 
669	stage, but this ability decreases during the competition stage. One may assume that the reason for this 
670	phenomenon is the increase in volume of intense distance work, which impairs the ability to produce explosive 
671	strength, because the latter plays a non-specific role in cyclic sports. Based on research and experience, the 
672	LDTE phenomenon may be characterised as follows (sec Fig 6.31):
673	1. Concentration of the volume of strength loading (A) over a limited period exerts an extensive, unidirectional 
674	training influence on the body. Concentration of strength loading is the basic condition for the beginning of 
675	the LDTE.
676	2. The lower the speed-strength levels fall (within an optimal range) during the concentration of strength loading 
677	stage, the higher they rise in the subsequent LDTE phase (graphs of Fl and F2). Excessive concentration of 
678	strength loading leads to a more significant drop in speed-strength and disruption of adaptation (graph F3).
679	363
680	
681	
682	######## PDF 375
683	SUPERTRAINING
684	3. When concentrated strength loading is used to elicit a LDTE, the selected means should not be intensive. 
685	Concentration of unidirectional loading already intensifies the training process, and one should not intensify 
686	it further with high intensity means.
687	4. A subsequent moderate volume of general developmental work, combined with special work of gradually 
688	increasing intensity contributes to eliciting the LDTE initiated by the concentrated strength loading (B).
689	5. The length of time for which the LDTE is displayed is determined by the volume and duration of the 
690	concentrated strength loading. In principle, the duration of the LDTE (T2) is approximately equal to the 
691	duration of the strength training stage (T 1). Under the actual training conditions o f highly qualified athletes, 
692	the LDTE was observed to last from 4-12 weeks during the long-term stages of strength preparation. 
693	However, one should bear in mind that appearance of the LDTE is individualised and to a large degree 
694	depends on the athlete's volume of loading and individual recuperative ability. An equivalent volume of 
695	loading for two athletes of the same qualification can yield significantly different effects.
696	There are a number of important circumstances associated with the production and use of the LDTE of strength 
697	loading during the annual cycle. Athletes invariably do not allow or do not have sufficient time for recuperation 
698	after extensive strength loading. Consequently, they minimise the possibility of stimulating a LDTE of strength 
699	loading and thereby maintain conditions which are extremely stressful for the body. Besides this, the body is 
700	regularly forced to unjustifiably deplete its current adaptation energy and sometimes draw upon its deep 
701	adaptation energy to restore its energy potential. Consequently, the effectiveness o f preparation is fairly low 
702	under such conditions and special work-capacity is not very high during the competition stage.
703	During the period of emergence of the LDTE of extensive strength loading, it is relatively easy and painless 
704	for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work. This is manifested in 
705	the slowed or even decreased growth of spced-strength. The volume of training work, therefore, should not be 
706	increased during the period of emergence of the LDTE. One should be especially cautious with strength loading 
707	during the competition period. At this time, intensive and short-term strength work can be used in a small 
708	volume to tone the neuromuscular system during competition preparation, as well as to maintain the achieved
709	364
710	
711	
712	######## PDF 376
713	SUPERTRAINING
714	level of speed-strcngth preparedness if the length of the competition period exceeds the duration of the LDTE of 
715	strength loading.
716	At this point it is relevant to comment on the relationship between strength training and technical training, 
717	especially since it has often been stressed that there seems to be no logical connection between these types of 
718	training. It should be noted that the competitive action executed with maximal physical exertion represents the 
719	most specific o f all the special training means. Therefore, this special means of training should be viewed 
720	simultaneously as a highly intense means of strength training and should occupy a placc of central importance in 
721	the training programme. In other words, a strength training programme should first be constructed in accordance 
722	with the principle of gradual increase in intensity and secondly, be combined with technique training so as to 
723	peak concurrently with the competitive act, performed with maximal effort.
724	At the highest level of sports mastery, improvement in performance is determined primarily by increasing the 
725	athlete’s special work capacity, which is essential for improving proficiency in any competitive event. Technical 
726	mastery is the ability to effectively realise one’s motor potential under competitive conditions. Increasing the 
727	level of special work capacity, in particular one’s strength potential, in turn, promotes improvement in technique. 
728	This is largely a result of the athlete becoming able to concentrate his effort more effectively, increase range of 
729	movement, decrease the time of execution of movements, improve his stability, improve the strength of muscular 
730	control over all movements and increase his resistance to fatigue. 
731	Thus, special physical preparation and 
732	technical training are closely linked and interdependent. However, the dominant role in this interaction is played 
733	by special physical preparation, both in the yearly cycle and in long-term training.
734	It should never be forgotten that high-volume strength loads are detrimental to one’s current level of speed- 
735	strength fitness and, consequently, to technical preparation. To avoid this, it is advisable in training high level 
736	athletes to structure the programme so that strength work precedes and does not interfere with technical training. 
737	Technical training should take place in the presence of the delayed training effect of the conccntrated volume of 
738	strength work, i.e. when there is recovery of work capacity and an increase in the level of speed-strength. 
739	Technique rapidly adjusts to the athlete's higher level of specialised work capacity and there is much less 
740	likelihood of reinforcing errors which may arise in connection with the body's lowered functional state, caused by 
741	high-volume loads. 
742	This type of programming, especially as part of the conjugate system of training, 
743	successively introduces different modes of loading into the training rather than separating them in time, so that 
744	each mode tends to gradually replace its predecessor.
745	The Delayed Training Effect and Long Duration Work
746	With respect to aerobic and anaerobic productivity, there is no experimental data that clearly documents 
747	occurrence of the LDTE phenomenon in cyclic distance training. The exceptions are cases of intense training 
748	under the lowered oxygen conditions of high altitude. Here, characteristics of the LDTE phenomenon have been 
749	observed in swimmers, with significant increases being measured in maximum aerobic capacity, the total volume 
750	of work which can be executed at the critical level of power, VO2 max and the onset of blood lactatc accu­
751	mulation (Vaitsekhovsky et al, 1974). These changes persisted for more than 4 weeks after 3 weeks of training at 
752	an altitude of 1700m above sea level, with a peak response taking placc about 1 week after the altitude training. 
753	All of the athletes in the study improved their results immediately after training at altitude.
754	Similar results were obtained with skaters who were first tested with 4 minutes on a cycle ergometer every 
755	week for 3 weeks at an altitude of 2250m, then with the same test for the next 3 weeks at sea level (Ivanov,
756	1977). At altitude, there was a decrease in mechanical efficiency and an increase in oxygen consumption, energy 
757	expenditure and lactate accumulation. After a return to sea level, it was found that the functional efficiency of the 
758	work exceeded the pre-experimental levels as a result of more economical metabolism and a significantly 
759	diminished amount of anaerobically produced ATP.
760	The stay at low-oxygen (hypobaric) conditions common to both experiments provided a very demanding 
761	training influence which provoked persistent disturbance of the body’s homeostasis and subsequent activation of 
762	its adaptive processes.
