(onset of blood lactate accumulation) and the results of control runs of 400m and 1200m, as well as in their 
sporting performances. During the summer competition stage Group 2 improved the 800m time by an average of 
4.8 seconds and the 1500m run by 6.3 seconds, whereas in Group 1, the improvements were 3.4 and 4.6 seconds, 
respectively.
This and other studies of the influence of training loads on functional indicators show that three levels of 
change in an athlete's fitness state during training may be identified:
1. A long-term level characterised by the steady rise in the athlete's special work-capacity. 
This level is 
associated with prolonged training periods of one or more years and its basis lies in long-term adaptation, 
promoted chiefly by the volume of loading.
2. A medium-term level characterised by less stable and readily reversible functional changes, the basis for 
which is compensatory adaptation. These changes are associated with lengthy training stages of up to 5-6 
months and, together with the volume of the load, are produced by the characteristics of its contents, in 
particular, the proportion of intensive means in the total volume of loading.
3. A short-term level characterised by brief, but not precisely measurable, changes in the functional indicators,
i.e. changes representing the body's acute reaction to the training load. These changes concern the micro- 
cycle and are elicited by the magnitude of the load, the intensity of loading, the individual ability of the 
athlete to endure the loading and his restorative capabilities. At this level, the dynamics of the functional 
indicators are largely random and at times unpredictable. This level is not determined by the adaptation of the 
first two levels and is important only for organisation of the microcycle and achievement of the immediate 
effect of the current loading.
One practical conclusion that can be drawn from these findings is that the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state 
during the annual cycle are controllable. The dependence of the dynamics of fitness on the contents, volume and 
organisation of the loading is determined by definite adaptive processes. 
Consequently, training should be 
structured by first of all taking into account the dynamics of the athlete's special physical preparedness (SPP) and 
controlling the degree of conformity of the training to the actual sporting dynamics required at each stage.
367


######## PDF 379
SUPERTRAINING
Mastering the ability to effectively programme the contents of training and regulate the dynamics of the athlete’s 
fitness state during training involves eliminating all weak links in the system of managing training and thereby 
significantly increasing the probability of achieving the intended level of sporting performance.
The art of controlling the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state consists, firstly, of achieving the necessary 
level of conditioning and, secondly, achieving it at the required time, as dictated by the competition calendar. 
Research shows that achievement of the second requirement is not especially complex. However, the probability 
of successfully achieving the first requirement is much smaller.
6.12 Principles of Programming and Organising Training
The basis of programming is the programme-objective approach, in accordance with which the contents, volume 
and organisation of training loads are determined by the objectives of the preparation (see Fig 6.8). The 
objectives consist of three main components:
• the desired improvement in performance
• the appropriate changcs in technical-tactical, psychological and competition preparedness
• the necessary modification of special physical preparedness.
In practice, the selection of a programming strategy is performed by means of a logical 'if-then' approach, which 
is understood in the following way: if one sets a specific and quantitatively defined goal, then the precise work 
and methods necessary to accomplish this goal constitute the appropriate strategy.
6.12.1 Forms of Constructing Training
Construction of training involves regulating its contents to provide the effective use of loading of different 
primary emphasis, i.e. the organisation of the contents over time, so that the required training effect occurs with a 
minimal expenditure of energy.
Consequently, time and organisation are two closely interdependent variables in the planning of training. 
The contents and organisation of training are dictated by the training objectives and the characteristics of 
adaptation to the intense muscular work deemed to be necessary for the given period. The time limitation 
imposed by the competition calendar and the duration of the energy supply from the current adaptation reserves 
affects the selection of the contents and organisation of training. Actual conditions do not always satisfy the 
optimal values of these variables. Therefore, programming of training requires creative flexibility based on the 
skill to anticipate the effect of any form of training and select its optimal variant.
It is appropriate now to examine the different forms of training against a background of research into the 
characteristics of adaptation to intense exercise and the principal trends produced by the given loading in the 
dynamics of the athlete's cxercise state. Two categories of training construction may be identified: one based on 
structural organisation and the other on time management. With respect to organisation, one has to consider the 
ways of combining loading of different primary emphasis as a basic condition for achieving a large training 
effect. With respect to time, one has to consider ways of regulating the loading within definite cycles and stages, 
as determined by the periodisation of training and the competition calendar.
6.12.2 Organisational Aspects of Structuring Training
There are essentially two basic different ways of organising training, namely the complcx and the conccntrated 
loading methods. Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several 
different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a 
given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training.
Complex training refers to the concurrent use of different training means in the same workout, microcycle or 
mesocycle. For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a 
complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during 
different sessions on the same day. If complex means are to be utilised, it is essential to understand fully how the 
different means and exercises interact with one another, as determined by the acute and delayed after-effects of 
each (discussed earlier in this chaptcr). In addition, the prescription of complex means depends on the individual, 
the level of proficiency of the athlete, the specific objective, and the stage of the training programme, especially 
the proximity to important competitions

# Acute vs. Delayed, and Particular vs. Cumulative: The Book's Taxonomy of Training Effect

**What it is** — The authors distinguish the acute (immediate) training effect (ATE), the
body's short-term improvement or deterioration in functional state right after a strength
means is applied, from the delayed training effect (DTE), the more stable adaptation that
follows once the volume of training influence is sufficient (cross-referenced forward to
chapter 6.7.1, not yet ingested in this pass). Whether the immediate reaction is
deterioration or improvement is said to depend on the exercise's energy cost, which
determines the rest interval needed before the next exercise: the interval can be lengthened
if more rest is needed, or optimally shortened to exploit a beneficial "superimposed
after-effect phenomenon." Separately, the authors distinguish the particular effect (from
one or more unidirectional means, reflecting the specificity of that means and regime) from
the cumulative effect (from a complex of multi-directional means), stating explicitly that
the cumulative effect is not simply the sum of the body's individual functional changes, but
"a complex of new forms of its motor potential" that still contains the specific
characteristics of the particular means used. The authors then state five generalizations
about the training effect of a complex of means: (1) the training effect of any means
diminishes as the athlete's special physical fitness increases; (2) the means used should
produce the optimal training effect relative to the athlete's current functional state; (3)
the after-effect of previous work alters the training effect of any subsequent methods; (4) the
training effect of a complex of means depends not only on the sum of the individual stimuli
but also on their combination, order of succession and intervals of separation; (5) the
content of special strength training should be a complex of specific stimuli that produces
the strength fitness required for the given sport, matched to the athlete's level of sports
mastery. (PDF pp. 215-216, printed pp. 204-205.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for the ATE/DTE split beyond the energy-cost-driven
rest-interval logic, and the claim that a cumulative effect is "not simply the sum" of
individual effects is stated, not derived. Inference: this is consistent with the general
principle that a training stimulus interacts with the body's current state (fatigue,
potentiation, prior adaptation) rather than acting as an independent, additive input, the
same logic that underlies
[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]] in the passage immediately
following this one.

**When to apply** — The book ties the ATE to rest-interval choice: the interval before the
next exercise may be increased if the body needs more rest, or optimally shortened if the
superimposed after-effect is exploited beneficially (PDF p. 215, printed p. 204).
Inference: use the particular/cumulative distinction to judge whether a training block's
variety is producing an integrated adaptation or just a list of separate, unintegrated
stimuli, and use the five generalizations as a checklist when building a multi-means
training complex.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual taxonomy, not an operational protocol. The book
gives no specific rest-interval numbers here and no method for judging in real time whether a
given ATE is potentiating or depleting; the fuller treatment is deferred to chapter 6.7.1,
which is pending in this ingest.

**Example** — Inference: a heavy squat set placed before sprint work can either potentiate
or depress the sprint, depending on load, rest interval and the athlete; the book's own
after-effect data (see [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]]
and [[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]]) show improvement with
the right interval. The ATE/DTE lens says to test which one you get, not assume it. The
book gives no specific case here.

# After a Concentrated Block, Unload and Wait: Gains Commonly Appear After a 1-3 Week Latency

**What it is** — The authors warn: "The system is not without its dangers, since concentrated loading is very stressful and, besides increasing the potential for overtraining, it can decrease motor qualities such as speed-strength. After a phase of emphasis on heavy strength training, there may be an increase in muscle stiffness and a loss of explosive strength, sporting skill or speed." Their rule, italicised in the original: "a diminished loading and restorative period has to be observed after a given concentrated loading phase to allow the body to supercompensate to the desired level of preparedness." The timing: "The gains elicited, for instance, by 4-8 week concentrated blocks of strength, speed-strength or speed training, may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 weeks, so it is essential for the athlete not to lose patience and hasten into the next concentrated phase without adequate restoration. Not only does premature imposition of concentrated loading suppress the delayed training effect of the previous stage, but it also lowers the effectiveness of future training" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "the conjugate sequence system is based on exploitation of the delayed training effect" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294), so the next block must start once that effect has appeared, not before. No physiological mechanism is given in this section. Inference: the authors frame the restorative period as supercompensation; the two-factor (fitness-fatigue) reading in this library would describe the same pattern as fatigue clearing to reveal fitness, and the book does not choose between them here.

**When to apply** — After any 4-8 week block that concentrates on one quality, plan a lower-load period before the next concentrated block. Inference: judge the block's result after the 1-3 week latency, not on the last day of loading. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred). Inference: the 1-3 week latency is a reason to leave slack between blocks in that roadmap, so a delayed gain is not cut short by the next block.

**When NOT to apply** — The 1-3 week figure is "most commonly," with no study named. It is a latency to the onset of gains. Chapter 6 gives a different number for a different quantity: the long-term delayed training effect "was observed to last from 4-12 weeks during the long-term stages of strength preparation," its duration "approximately equal to the duration of the strength training stage," and its appearance "individualised" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image). **Contested across the library:** Bompa & Haff (5th ed.), not Supertraining, write that "Siff and Verkhoshansky (83) suggested that performance gains may occur 4 to 12 weeks after the cessation of the concentrated loading phase" (Bompa & Haff 5e, PDF idx 60 / printed p. 49), and the Bompa entry [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] repeats this as a 4-12 week delay. Bompa & Haff also say that "the greater the magnitude and duration of the concentrated loading phase, the more time needed for fatigue to dissipate and performance to improve" (same page, refs 83, 91, 103, 104). Inference: read as a 4-12 week wait before gains, the Bompa & Haff sentence matches neither Supertraining statement: 5.3.3 gives a 1-3 week latency to gains (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294), and Chapter 6 gives 4-12 weeks as how long the delayed effect lasts (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364). Read as the window in which gains show, it is close to the Chapter 6 figure. Fig 6.31 on that page (checked against the page image) shows the timing: the trained qualities (F1-F3) are depressed during the concentrated loading stage T1 and climb during T2, which begins where T1 ends (dashed line). The other 4-12 week figures in the book are also durations: Chapter 6 calls unidirectional training "for prolonged stages (4-12 weeks)" very effective (PDF p. 381 / printed p. 370, text layer), and the Addendum says "the tendency has been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks," with the delayed effect's duration "equal to the duration of the stage" (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, text layer). Use the onset figure for when to expect a result and the duration figure for how long it may hold. Chapter 6 also qualifies the warning: during the emergence of the delayed effect "it is relatively easy and painless for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364), so the restorative period is about volume, not a full stop.

**Example** — The authors' own: after a 4-8 week concentrated strength block, the gains "may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 weeks" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294). Inference: an off-season strength block ending in late March would be judged in April, and the speed-emphasis block that follows would open at lower volume rather than at full load.

**Related** — [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the delayed training effect), [[case-study--deniskin-depth-jumps-after-resistance-and-rest-as-a-training-means]] (rest weeks between stages), [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear]] (4.1.1, speed-strength up 18-25% after a 10-day rest, PDF p. 213; an in-library case for a short latency), [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]

**Related** — [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the delayed training effect), [[case-study--deniskin-depth-jumps-after-resistance-and-rest-as-a-training-means]] (rest weeks between stages), [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear]] (4.1.1, speed-strength up 18-25% after a 10-day rest, PDF p. 213; an in-library case for a short latency), [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]

Exit code 1
# When Concentrated Unidirectional Loading Works: A Diverse Complex of Means, Low-Intensity Means, and 23-25% of the Year's Volume in One Month

**What it is** — The authors set out the working conditions for the concentrated phases of the conjugate sequence system (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294, checked against the page image):
1. **Scale and duration.** "Unidirectional emphasis on qualities such as strength or endurance may be used not only in individual workouts but also during each microcycle (Kudelin, 1980; Budokho et al, 1978; Mironenko, 1980). Research has shown that unidirectional training over periods as long as 4-12 weeks can be very effective, especially if the intensity is gradually increased for each form of loading in the given cycle."
2. **Diversity within one emphasis.** "unidirectional loading is effective only if one uses a diverse complex of means with a single primary emphasis, together with a variety of training methods (Fedorova et al, 1975; Platonov & Monograov, 1977; Verkhoshansky, 1977)."
3. **Low intensity of the means.** "an important condition for implementing concentrated loading is the relatively low intensity of the means, since the frequent use of these means already intensifies the training."

# A Structured Complex of Means Beats Volume Alone or a Random Combination of the Same Means

**What it is** — The authors define training load by five characteristics: its resulting
effect (the qualitative and quantitative special work capacity produced), its composition or
contents (the complex of means applied), its structure (the correlation of means), its volume
(the quantity of training work) and its intensity (the difficulty or quality of the work).
They argue that raising training volume alone cannot compensate for a low training effect
from the means being used, but also that there is no guarantee that highly effective,
logically organized specialized means can produce the same special work capacity at a much
smaller volume in less time. They add that "the volume of the load is undoubtedly one of the
conditions for raising the special work capacity in many sport[s] (chiefly the cyclic types)
during specific stages of preparation" (the scan clips the right margin). Training volume is said to serve two functions: providing a
functional base for further development of special work capacity (called a universal
principle) and raising special fitness primarily through endurance development (said to be
appropriate only for certain sports). The text also states a direct correlation between
training volume and how long a training effect is maintained, and calls volume an important
condition for successful technical preparation. On structure, the authors state that "no one
means or method of special preparation should be considered universal or absolutely
effective"; each means should have its own place in a training stage depending on the sport's
specificity, the athlete's fitness level, prior training loads and the current stage's aims.
Citing Verkhoshansky (1966, 1970), Tatyan (1974) and Khodykin (1975), the authors state that
special strength training using a specific, structured system of different means and methods
produces a significantly greater effect than randomly using the same means and methods
separately, an advantage achieved even at a smaller volume of work. (PDF p. 217, printed
p. 206.)

Figure 4.1 (PDF p. 214, printed p. 203, section 4.1.1) is a separate illustration, captioned
"The introduction of different means with higher training effect (Verkhoshansky, 1977)." The
text calls it "the basic scheme of special strength training ... where A, B and C are
training means of successively greater training effect for a given athlete." It shows three
curves from a common origin, labelled "Means A" (lowest), "Means B" and "Means C" (highest),
with specific training effect on the y-axis and performance on the x-axis; each curve rises
and flattens at a successively higher level. The plot's x-axis is performance, not time.
That the means are introduced in sequence comes from the text: "with growth in sporting
proficiency, it is necessary to determine the sequence for introducing the chosen means into
the training process by calculating the growth and continuity of their training effect."
The same page adds that "The contribution of different training means to developing the key
motor abilities diminishes with improvement in athletic results," and that the means "are
different in terms of their training effect and the use of each of them is justified only
when the athlete's level of fitness is taken into consideration." (PDF p. 214, printed
p. 203.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why a structured, logically-ordered
combination outperforms a random combination at equal or lower volume; the cited studies
(Verkhoshansky 1966, 1970; Tatyan 1974; Khodykin 1975) are not described in this passage
beyond the summary claim. Inference: this is consistent with the non-commutative and
non-associative framing given in the same section
([[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]): if order and combination
change outcomes, a deliberately structured combination should on average outperform a
randomly-ordered one of equal volume, simply by avoiding combinations that interfere with
each other.

**When to apply** — Inference: when training volume cannot be increased further, whether
from time, recovery capacity, or in-season constraints, prioritize reorganizing the
composition, structure and intensity of the training complex over adding more work. Use
Figure 4.1's logic to plan which means (for example, general strength work, then specialized
strength work, then reactive or plyometric work) to introduce as the training effect from the
prior means saturates for that athlete.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a general planning heuristic, not a specific protocol. The
book gives no criteria for identifying, in practice, when a given means has "saturated" for
an individual athlete, and the cited studies are Soviet-era citations not described in enough
detail here to assess their design or effect size.

**Example** — Inference: a program that keeps adding sets of the same exercises indefinitely
to chase more volume, without varying composition or structure as the athlete adapts, is the
failure mode this heuristic warns against. Figure 4.1's "Means A" curve, which levels off at the
lowest ceiling, represents that means running out of training effect, at which point a
different means ("Means B" or "Means C") is needed to keep raising the athlete's specific
training effect. The book gives no worked case.

**Related** — [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]],
[[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]],
[[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]],
[[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/principle--accommodation-and-the-diminishing-returns-law]]; [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]] (5.3, the systematic use of means gives a cumulative effect greater than their separate, non-sequential use; it cites this entry's point that a structured complex beats volume); [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]] (5.4.4, bring in more effective means as each one's training effect fades; it cites this entry's Fig 4.1); [[principle--sequentially-introduce-means-of-greater-training-effect]] (5.3.2, the sequential rule: each means' training effect should match current fitness and rise with it)
-----
16:**What it is** — The authors report a set of experiments on novices in speed-strength sports (researchers named as "Purvin, Khodykin, Deniskin, Tatian and Chernousov", names checked against the page image; no dates, sample sizes or statistics are given) (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288):
30:**Related** — [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]], [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]] (the conclusions the authors draw), [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the after-effect within a session), [[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]], [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]], [[claim--depth-jump-training-beat-higher-volume-traditional-training-in-jumpers]] (5.2.4, the resistance-before-plyometrics rule), [[heuristic--brief-maximal-tension-vs-plyometrics-by-resi

**What it is** — The authors report a set of experiments on novices in speed-strength sports (researchers named as "Purvin, Khodykin, Deniskin, Tatian and Chernousov", names checked against the page image; no dates, sample sizes or statistics are given) (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288):
1. **Order across the preparatory period.** "the sequence of means in the preparatory period (beginning with strength, then speed-strength means, or vice-versa) has no real significance for novices. Consequently, the same effect can be obtained by using these means in any order."
2. **Mixed sessions.** "A relatively larger effect than produced by the above-mentioned variants (with the same volume of training load) occurred in groups who used strength and speed-strength means concurrently by alternating them in mixed training sessions" (the mixed regime used separate sessions "with a rest interval between sessions on the same day", PDF p. 299). The authors add that "the contrasting of stimuli in mixed workouts ... undoubtedly has a positive effect."
3. **Weights then depth jumps.** One novice group did weights in stage 1 and depth jumps in stage 2, a second the reverse, a third both in both stages (not in the same workout). "the first variant was more effective for developing speed-strength." The concurrent group improved in stage 1 but slowed in stage 2 "due to monotonous repetition"; the reversed group improved most after stage 1 but its speed-strength "were lowest at the end of the second stage."
4. **Within one workout.** Strength-then-speed-strength vs the reverse, with pauses "increased slightly to minimise the influence of the positive after-effect", plus a depth-jump group: "There was no statistically significant difference in speed-strength of the subjects in the first two groups. The largest increase in all the parameters of the control movement was discovered in the third group." Depth jumps gave "significantly larger improvement in speed-strength fitness for a smaller volume of training."

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for experiment 4: "any training influence will leave significant traces in an untrained person. The body is unable to react selectively to a chiefly strength or speed-strength means in one workout. In addition, the period over which the traces of the training stimulus are maintained is apparently longer than the duration of the after-effect of prior tonic work. Within one workout, the traces of all the training tasks are summed" (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288). For experiment 3, the reversed group's early gain is put down to "the larger training effect of the plyometric method." No mechanism is given for the "monotonous repetition" slowdown.

content.content:
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
tremely concentrated loads lead to a more significant decrease in functional indices and to a 
disruption in adaptation (graph fj).
When using concentrated loads orientated to achieving the LDTE, the methods used should 
not be extremely intense. Concentration, in one of the single purpose loads, is already in­
tensification of the training effect and to increase it with highly intense means of training 
does not follow.
Realization of LDTE of concentrated loads is served by moderate increases in work volume 
and gradually increasing intensity (B).
. 
The duration of the appearance of LDTE is determined by the volume and duration of the 
concentrated loads used. In principle, the steady appearance of LDTE (t2 ) is equal to the du­
ration of the stage (ti). In real conditions of training high level athletes, the tendency has 
been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks. It follows, however, to keep in mind 
that the appearance of LDTE has an independent character and to a significant degree, de­
pends upon the ability of the athlete to withstand volume loads and the ability of his body 
for recovery. The same volume loads in two athletes having the same qualifications can 
have a different effect.
>. 
In the period of LDTE realization, volume concentrated loads are handled by the body rela­
tively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work 
volume. The latter is expressed by a slowdown in increases and even a decrease in the func­
tional abilities. For example. Figure 8 shows that in triple jumpers, after the concentrated 
specialized strength preparation loads in March-April, the LDTE acquired showed an in­
crease in speed-strength and increased sports results in May-June.
iowever, an insignificant increase in their volume in specialized strength preparation (by only a 
ew percent) in order to “maintain” the achieved level of specialized workability (as believed by 
he athlete) led to a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results. As a result of this, the ath- 
ete lost his chance to be selected in the qualifying competitions for a place on the national team, 
fhe phenomenon of LDTE of concentrated loads should be looked at as an important base qual-
Figure 7 - The principal scheme of the Long Lasting training effect of the concentrated strength loads:
A - the stage of the concentrated loads; ti - duration of this stage;
B - the stage of the specific training loads

=== periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching
confidence: supported
**What it is** — A short period of deliberately high, "saturated" training load on one quality (planned overreaching), followed by restitution. Performance is *suppressed* during the loading block and rebounds — supercompensates — afterward. Bompa & Haff cite Siff and Verkhoshansky for gains **4 to 12 weeks** after the concentrated block ends (Bompa & Haff 5e, printed p. 49); *Supertraining* itself gives a 1-3 week latency before gains appear and 4-12 weeks as how long the delayed effect lasts (see [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]]). Bompa & Haff's own rule (same page): the longer/larger the loading, the longer the delay 
=== periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle
confidence: supported
**What it is** — After a training stimulus the body passes through four phases: (I) fatigue/homeostasis drop, 1–2 hr; (II) compensation/recovery, 24–48 hr; (III) supercompensation — a rebound *above* baseline, ~36–72 hr; (IV) involution — the gain fades if no new stimulus arrives, 3–7 days. Training the next stimulus into the supercompensation window raises the homeostatic set-point over time. Also called Weigert's law; Bompa links it to Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm → resistance → exhaustion).

content.content:
**What it is** — Issurin extends the concentration principle to single-session design
(Figure 2.4, PDF p. 74, printed p. 63; Table 2.12, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65) with five
stated rules (PDF p. 75, printed p. 64): (1) a workout should contain **no more than three
training modalities**, typically one dominant, one compatible with the main purpose, and
one for technique/tactics improvement or restoration; (2) **65-70% of total training time**
in a development workout should go to one or two selected modalities, to preserve workload
concentration; (3) the typical frequency of workouts in high-performance training (6-12 a
week) dictates certain conditions for the session after a key-workout: it should show a
significant load reduction, and running two consecutive key-workouts, while possible, risks
excessive load concentration; (4) hypertrophy-focused sessions require workload to be
"substantially reduced" for **at least 20 hours** afterward to protect the anabolic phase of
muscle restoration; (5) limiting modality count matters most in high-performance sport; the
daily program for juniors, for example, may be more diverse, multilateral, and therefore
more attractive. Figure 2.4 maps which modalities are compatible as secondary/tertiary
additions to five dominant ones: aerobic endurance pairs with alactic sprint,
strength-endurance-aerobic, and hypertrophy-strength (placed after); anaerobic glycolytic
endurance pairs with strength-endurance-anaerobic, aerobic restoration, and mixed
aerobic-anaerobic endurance; alactic sprint pairs with aerobic endurance, explosive
strength, hypertrophy-strength (after), and aerobic restoration; hypertrophy-strength pairs
with neural-strength, flexibility, and aerobic restoration; and, when learning new technical
elements is the dominant task, any kind of training modality may be added, but only *after*
the dominant, technical-learning task, not before it. Table 2.12 gives the
physiological/psychological rationale for
several of the strongest pairings (e.g., aerobic endurance + strength endurance: increased
oxidation supports the resistance work; alactic sprint + aerobic endurance: brief sprints
break monotony and keep a wide muscle-fiber pool activated for the subsequent aerobic work).

**Why it works: the specific numeric thresholds are asserted, not derived** — The
underlying logic is the same concentration principle from Chapter 1
([[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]): splitting a session across too many

**What it is** — Bondarchuk states that most athletes, after a rest/transition period,
take 2-3 months to enter a state of "sports form" in whatever exercises they are doing,
though some individuals take "4-7 and even 8 months" (PDF p. 39, printed p. 22). A
general-preparation stage/block can only function as a real "base" or "foundation" for the
following specialized stage if it lasts at least as long as that individual's own
sports-form development timeline. He gives his own worked numbers for how this plays out:
in a single-cycle training year, the general-preparation stage runs "on the average, three
months," long enough to let most athletes actually enter sports form in it; in a two-cycle
year, the second general-preparation stage shrinks to "4-6 weeks," and in a three-cycle
year to "2-3 weeks", both too short for athletes to "have time to enter into full sports
form in the exercises used." (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) He gives a
worked counter-example: a sprint/hurdle program with a 10-day general-endurance stage, a
15-day general-strength stage, a 6-8 week speed/speed-endurance stage, and a 2-3 week
entry-into-form stage. Because the first two stages are far shorter than the 2-3+ months
needed to reach sports form, he argues it is "impossible to resolve" real development of
general endurance or general strength in that time; those stages become mere "followers"
(tag-alongs) that prep the body for the next stage, not genuine developmental blocks in
their own right, and sports form only actually begins developing once the speed/speed-
endurance stage starts. (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) Only stage, block,
stage-variant, and block-variant methods (which run long enough) can create a real
transferable base; very short 1-3 week rotating stages cannot produce "distant" transfer
of a created base; only "current" transfer is possible under those short-cycle designs
(see [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]]). (PDF pp. 40-42, printed pp.
23-25.)

# The Long-Term Delayed Training Effect: Volume Well Above the Optimum Depresses Speed-Strength, Then a Timed Volume Cut Lets It Rise Above Baseline

**What it is** — The authors report "a steady decrease in speed-strength preparedness during individual training stages of different length (from 5-12 weeks)" caused by "voluminous strength loading," after which "speed-strength returns to its initial level and significantly exceeds it" (Nikitin 1977; Mironenko 1979; Antonova 1982; Levchenko 1982). Because this "does not agree with established ideas which stipulate a continuous rise in special physical preparedness" and "is not accompanied by marked signs of overtraining," it became "a subject of special study" (PDF p. 374 / printed p. 363, checked against the page image). They then state a dose-response rule: "The volume of the training load has a definite optimum level for each athlete, above or below which the body reacts with diminished response." "If the volume of loading is lower than the optimum level, special work-capacity decreases after some initial rise. If the volume of loading significantly exceeds this level, a steady decrease in special work-capacity occurs which, however, rises intensely during the carefully-timed reduction in the volume. # Put Technical Training in the Delayed-Effect Window, and Keep Competition-Period Strength Work Short, Intense and Small

**What it is** — Three linked rules from 6.10:
1. **Strength first, technique in the rebound.** "high-volume strength loads are detrimental to one's current level of speed-strength fitness and, consequently, to technical preparation. To avoid this, it is advisable in training high level athletes to structure the programme so that strength work precedes and does not interfere with technical training. Technical training should take place in the presence of the delayed training effect of the concentrated volume of strength work, i.e. when there is recovery of work capacity and an increase in the level of speed-strength." Technique then "rapidly adjusts to the athlete's higher level of specialised work capacity and there is much less likelihood of reinforcing errors" from the "lowered functional state, caused by high-volume loads" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image).
2. **Do not add volume while the effect emerges.** "The volume of training work, therefore, should not be increased during the period of emergence of the LDTE" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image).
3. **Competition period.** "One should be especially cautious with strength loading during the competition period. At this time, intensive and short-term strength work can be used in a small volume to tone the neuromuscular system during competition preparation, as well as to maintain the achieved level of speed-strength preparedness if the length of the competition period exceeds the duration of the LDTE of strength loading" (PDF pp. 375-376 / printed pp. 364-365).

The authors also state that "the competitive action executed with maximal physical exertion represents the most specific of all the special training means," to be viewed "simultaneously as a highly intense means of strength training," so a strength programme should rise in intensity and be "combined with technique training so as to peak concurrently with the competitive act" (PDF p. 376). They give "the dominant role" in the strength-technique interaction to "special physical preparation, both in the yearly cycle and in long-term training" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons: a strength-depressed state reinforces technical errors, while a higher work capacity lets the athlete "concentrate his effort more effectively, increase range of movement, decrease the time of execution of movements, improve his stability, improve the strength of muscular control over all movements and increase his resistance to fatigue" (PDF p. 376). For rule 2 they report that during emergence "it is relatively easy and painless for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work," seen as "slowed or even decreased growth of speed-strength" (PDF p. 375).

**When to apply** — After a concentrated strength block, schedule the heaviest technical emphasis for the weeks when speed-strength is coming back up, and hold volume flat through that period. In a long competition period, keep a small dose of intense, brief strength work. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: rule 3 says the same thing for the competition period. Eric's baseline: the in-season week has "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: that sits with rule 3's "small volume" and "short-term" strength work; the authors give no day-level timing.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** The Addendum restates the emergence-period rule the other way round: "In the period of LDTE realization, volume concentrated loads are handled by the body relatively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work volume" (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, text layer only). Its own example then agrees with Chapter 6: triple jumpers whose specialised strength volume rose "by only a few percent" to "maintain" their level saw "a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results" (same page, text layer). Inference: the Addendum sentence may be a translation slip, since its example fits Chapter 6, but the book prints both. The authors give no number for "small volume" or for how long technical emphasis should wait. Inference: for skills that need daily practice (team-sport play), technique cannot simply wait for the strength block to end; the rule is written for "high level athletes" in events where the competitive action can be isolated, and they mention the conjugate system "successively introduces different modes of loading ... rather than separating them in time" (PDF p. 376), so the separation is a matter of emphasis.

**Example** — The authors' own, from the Addendum (text layer, PDF p. 536): triple jumpers gained speed-strength and results in May-June after concentrated specialised strength loads in March-April, then lost both quickly when they raised strength volume by a few percent to hold the gain. Inference: an off-season strength block ending in March would hand over to technical and speed emphasis in April with strength volume held, not raised.

# For Aerobic and Anaerobic Productivity, a Long-Term Delayed Effect Has Been Documented Only After Altitude Training

**What it is** — Under "The Delayed Training Effect and Long Duration Work," the authors state: "With respect to aerobic and anaerobic productivity, there is no experimental data that clearly documents occurrence of the LDTE phenomenon in cyclic distance training. The exceptions are cases of intense training under the lowered oxygen conditions of high altitude" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image). Their evidence:
- **Swimmers (Vaitsekhovsky et al 1974).** "significant increases" in "maximum aerobic capacity, the total volume of work which can be executed at the critical level of power, VO2 max and the onset of blood lactate accumulation." "These changes persisted for more than 4 weeks after 3 weeks of training at an altitude of 1700m above sea level, with a peak response taking place about 1 week after the altitude training. All of the athletes in the study improved their results immediately after training at altitude."
- **Skaters (Ivanov 1977).** A 4-minute cycle-ergometer test weekly for 3 weeks at 2250 m, then for 3 weeks at sea level. At altitude, mechanical efficiency fell and oxygen consumption, energy expenditure and lactate rose; back at sea level, "the functional efficiency of the work exceeded the pre-experimental levels as a result of more economical metabolism and a significantly diminished amount of anaerobically produced ATP" (same page).
- **Swimmers under large loads (Susman 1978).** Large loads slowed "complex motor reactions," reduced precision of movement patterns and of "tracking a moving object," and lowered work capacity, ECG-assessed cardiovascular state, muscle tonus and adrenal-cortex hormone levels. After loads were reduced and intensity altered, these indicators rose "as the supercompensation (adaptive reconstruction) phase emerged" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for the altitude cases: hypobaric conditions gave "a very demanding training influence which provoked persistent disturbance of the body's homeostasis and subsequent activation of its adaptive processes" (PDF p. 376). For why the LDTE is not seen at sea level, they hedge: if it exists there, the disturbance "will occur at the level of more subtle physiological systems" not detectable by "methods used for assessing the more gross aerobic and anaerobic processes," and "adaptation apparently occurs at deeper cellular and molecular levels (e.g. in the mitochondria and endocrine system)" (Yakovlev 1957, 1974; Viru 1969, 1981; Finogenov 1979), while "disturbance of homeostasis can be detected in the dynamics of a number of psycho-physiological indicators" of the central nervous and neuromuscular systems (PDF pp. 376-377). This is a stated hypothesis, not a demonstrated mechanism.

**When to apply** — When planning or interpreting altitude camps: the book's one quantified case puts the peak about 1 week after a 3-week stay, with changes lasting more than 4 weeks. When judging a heavy endurance block: the authors point to psycho-physiological and neuromuscular indicators as the place a hidden disturbance may show. Eric's baseline: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: a neuromuscular marker of that kind is the sort of indicator the authors suggest, though they name reaction, precision and tracking tasks, not jump tests.

**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no sample sizes, controls or statistics for any of the three studies, and the skater study has no non-altitude comparison group in the text. The authors say plainly that the LDTE in sea-level distance training is not documented; do not carry the strength-block LDTE timings ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]) over to aerobic work. The LDTE they do report in cyclic sports (middle-distance running, swimming, skating) follows concentrated strength loading and shows in strength-endurance measures, not in aerobic productivity (PDF p. 374). Inference: altitude camps are rare in American collegiate football, so this entry matters mainly for endurance or Olympic-sport programmes.

**Example** — The authors' own: swimmers after 3 weeks at 1700 m improved immediately, peaked about 1 week after returning, and kept the gains for more than 4 weeks (Vaitsekhovsky et al 1974; PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365).

# Distributed and Concentrated Loading Both Work at Medium Qualification; Highly Qualified Athletes Need Concentration

**What it is** — For loading of one primary emphasis, the authors separate "distributed loading," "a relatively uniform distribution of means during an annual cycle," from "concentrated loading," "the concentration of means over definite training stages" (PDF p. 371 / printed p. 360, checked against the page image). Their claim: "Research indicates that both methods are successful in training athletes of medium qualification. The concentrated loading method is appropriate for the training of highly qualified athletes." The evidence named: "distribution of glycolytic work over the annual cycle of highly qualified sprinters raises the loading volume, but does not increase the effectiveness of the loading. However, by concentrating the volume of glycolytic work at certain stages, the work can be executed at a smaller volume but with a more significant improvement in speed-endurance (Kornelyuk, 1980)." "Similar results" are reported for concentrated special strength work in sprinters (Levchenko 1986), middle-distance runners (Sirenko & Zhdanovich 1982), boxers (Filimonov 1979) and jumpers (Mironenko & Antonova 1981). Their conclusion, italicised in the original: "concentration of the volume of uni-directional loading produces more extensive functional changes and greater improvement in the athlete's physical fitness" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "The regular use of training with distributed loading which is dispersed over a prolonged period evokes only a transient functional reaction which does not enhance the development of long-term adaptation. Distributed loading initially can yield some rise in functional level but its training potential soon drops because of rapid adaptation of the body to the training stimuli" (PDF p. 371). No physiological mechanism beyond that is given.

**When to apply** — For advanced athletes whose progress has stalled under an even, year-round spread of one kind of work, concentrate that work into defined stages. The authors list concentration of loading over time among their four organisational principles of special strength training (PDF pp. 370-371). # Within One Session, the Order of Paired Explosive-Strength Means Matters Less Than Their Volume and Contrast

**What it is** — For explosive strength, the authors list "brief combinations of training means" that give "a positive cumulative effect": "short and long jumping exercises"; "barbell exercises and jumping exercises"; "barbell exercises with 30% and 90% of maximum"; "barbell exercises and the plyometric method of developing explosive-strength"; "leaping with kettle-bells and jumping exercises"; "barbell exercises and leaping with kettle-bells" (PDF p. 371 / printed p. 360, checked against the page image). Then: "In a single training session the order of the above means, combined in a systematic complex is fairly unimportant, since the length of time for which the body maintains the after-effect of training stress exceeds the duration of the workout." In italics: "concerning the development of explosive strength, the order of the means is not fundamentally as important as the volume of the loading and the degree of contrast between the different training means." Yet in the next sentence: "Nevertheless, one should still preserve the above order of combining means in each case, since this provides the favourable effect of a brief rise in fitness state, which the first exercise produces as the second one is executed (see Ch 5.3)." Their delivery rule: "employ them sequentially with active rest between each series," and when repeating a series, "vary the exercises to avoid monotony and to maintain the optimal rest interval" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "During this session and the subsequent restoration period, a generalised summation of the after-effects of the entire complex of training influences of different primary emphasis occurs, which produces the same cumulative effect, generally regardless of their sequence" (PDF p. 371). They add that "it is still sensible to apply the recommended scheme of Figure 1.7 to minimise the risk of reducing skill and safety." Figure 1.7 in this edition is a torque diagram in 1.2 (PDF pp. 28-29, text layer), so that cross-reference appears to be wrong and the intended scheme is unclear.

**When to apply** — Building a contrast or complex session for explosive strength from one of the listed pairs: settle the volume and the contrast between the two means first, then keep the listed order as a secondary choice. Inference: when equipment or space forces the order to flip on a given day, the authors' text says little is lost within the session. Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)).

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** The same page says order is "fairly unimportant" and then that "one should still preserve the above order." Chapter 5 states the order flatly the other way in one place and the same way in another: "Strength exercises should be done after speed-strength exercises in training" (PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290), while 5.2.4 says resistance plus plyometrics works best "provided the resistance movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277). # Which Endurance Loads Help or Hurt the Load That Follows, and How Long Restoration Takes

**What it is** — The authors first warn that for endurance, research on the interaction of loads of different emphasis is "inadequate" and "often so contradictory that it is very difficult to discern definite trends" (PDF pp. 371-372 / printed pp. 360-361, checked against the page images). The energy-system categories (aerobic, alactic-anaerobic, anaerobic-glycolytic, mixed) "are so conditional that they permit very broad interpretation" and "cannot be strictly applied" to judging a load's emphasis, and "no research has analysed the energy processes occurring while the general activity is undoubtedly aerobic, but the postural muscles are strongly contracted" (PDF p. 372). With that caveat, "current experimental data indicates" (PDF p. 372, checked against the page image):

Positive interaction, where "the previous loading creates favourable conditions for executing the subsequent loading and raises the effect of the training session as a whole":
- "aerobic exercises are done after ATP-CP training"
- "aerobic exercises are done after glycolytic-anaerobic training (in small volume)"
- "glycolytic-anaerobic exercises are done after ATP-CP training."

Negative interaction (Volkov 1975):
- "ATP-CP exercises are done after a large amount of any glycolytic work"
- "glycolytic-anaerobic exercises follow large volumes of aerobic work."

Restoration figures: after "a large volume of aerobic work," restoration of energy resources and endocrine equilibrium "is prolonged by 2-3 days," during which "a small volume of anaerobic loading" is appropriate and "will not negatively influence the restoration of aerobic capacity." "Restoration after moderate volumes of anaerobic loading usually takes 3-8 hours," "very large volumes of anaerobic loading will delay restoration," and "The training effect of ATP-CP workouts deteriorates if the sessions are done without allowing full restoration from the preceding loading" (Nabatnikova 1972; Volkov 1975; Platonov 1980; PDF p. 372). On the next page they add: "the rest pause is actually a training means which is just as important as muscular work" (italics in the original; PDF p. 373 / printed p. 362, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' only stated reason is the one above: the earlier load either sets up or spoils the conditions for the later one. They give no physiological mechanism for each pairing. Inference: the pattern reads as "keep the highest-power work fresh and put the longer, lower-power work after it," but that is a summary, not the book's explanation.

**When to apply** — Ordering conditioning within a session or across consecutive days: alactic work before glycolytic or aerobic work; aerobic work after a small glycolytic dose; no alactic speed work after a big glycolytic session; a small anaerobic dose is acceptable in the 2-3 days after a big aerobic session. Eric's baseline: "All three energy systems ... are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 114, Explicit). Inference: the authors' warning that the categories are "so conditional" agrees with that line. Eric's baseline: the football priority stack is "alactic and aerobic capacity/power" with glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" (line 116, Explicit; Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the positive pairing "aerobic exercises are done after ATP-CP training" fits that two-system stack in one session.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves call the endurance evidence inadequate and contradictory, give no sample sizes, and cite only the negative list to one author (Volkov 1975). "Large," "small" and "moderate" volumes are not quantified. Inference: the 3-8 hour and 2-3 day figures are general restoration estimates, not limits for a given athlete. The positive list is about order within or between sessions; it is not the same as the long-term sequence across stages ([[framework--three-viewpoints-on-organising-endurance-development]]).

**Example** — Inference: a football off-season day of short acceleration sprints followed by tempo running fits "aerobic exercises are done after ATP-CP training"; reversing it, with a long glycolytic conditioning test before sprint work, fits the negative case "ATP-CP exercises are done after a large amount of any glycolytic work." The authors give no worked session.

**Related** — [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-organising-endurance-development]], [[heuristic--within-session-order-of-explosive-means-matters-less-than-volume-and-contrast]], [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]], [[block-periodization--issurin/principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]] (Issurin's Fig 2.4 also pairs alactic sprint with aerobic endurance), [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--aerobic-anaerobic-energy-system-transfer-asymmetry]]

# Sequential Stages Need 4-6 Weeks to Count: Extensive Submaximal Resistance First, Then Explosive Work

**What it is** — "Sequential accumulation of the training effect of loading of different primary emphasis has a place in long-term preparation and is achieved by the action of preceding work on subsequent work" (PDF p. 372 / printed p. 361, checked against the page image). For explosive strength, "positive accumulation is achieved by means of a sequence which applies extensive (i.e. high volume) training with submaximal resistance first, followed by explosive training," and "The reverse sequence of this loading scheme leads to a negative cumulative effect." The time rule: "The mechanism of sequential accumulation is appropriate only if the training effect of the previous work has become relatively stable, which takes at least 4-6 weeks. When the strength means of different emphasis are changed over shorter time intervals, for example after 2 weeks, the body cannot differentiate between the specifics of their individual influence and the body's adaptive reaction as mediated by the transient accumulation process. Thus, a change after 2-week stages of use in the order of loading of different emphasis minimally alters the resulting training effect" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors give a mechanism for the order: "the positive accumulation is achieved by the first loading regime producing a rise in the general energy potential of the neuromuscular system. This creates favourable conditions for further adaptation, facilitated by the subsequent loading" (PDF p. 372). For the 4-6 week rule, their reason is that shorter stages blur into "transient accumulation" (the form defined in [[framework--temporal-and-qualitative-forms-of-the-training-effect]]); no data or study is named for the 4-6 week figure.

**When to apply** — Planning an off-season run of strength and explosive stages: put the high-volume submaximal strength stage first, hold it at least 4-6 weeks, then switch to explosive emphasis. Inference: rotating emphasis every 2 weeks gives a mixed (transient) effect rather than a sequence, so if a coach wants a true sequence the stages should be longer; if a mixed effect is wanted, short rotation is acceptable. Eric's baseline: "The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 180, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: that order matches the book's extensive-then-explosive sequence.

**When NOT to apply** — The 4-6 week figure is stated without a cited study. The authors' own Fig 6.24 experiment used 3-month stages ([[case-study--barbell-and-depth-jump-sequences-in-high-jumpers]]), so the 4-6 weeks is a minimum, not a tested optimum. Eric's baseline: "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... waving volume week to week" is Eric's preferred model (line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: by this passage, week-to-week waves inside one emphasis are compatible with the rule, but changing the emphasis itself every two weeks would be the "transient" case. Bondarchuk agrees on the direction, from a different premise: stages shorter than the 2-3 months most athletes need to reach sports form cannot build a real base, and 1-3 week rotating stages give only "current" transfer ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle]]). Inference: Issurin's accumulation blocks of up to about six weeks, and shorter ones to refresh ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]]), concern block length for a mixed set of targets, a different quantity from the 4-6 week stability threshold here.

**Example** — The authors' own direction: extensive submaximal resistance work first, then explosive training; the reverse gives "a negative cumulative effect" (PDF p. 372). Inference: a 6-week high-volume squat and pull stage at moderate loads, then a 4-6 week jump and light-load speed stage, rather than alternating the two emphases every fortnight.

# Three Viewpoints on Building Endurance Across the Year: Concurrent, Sequential, and Concurrent With a Shifting Emphasis

**What it is** — The authors first set two conditions that make endurance sequencing "more complex" than explosive-strength sequencing: in cyclic sports "the fundamental sport activity is traditionally the chief means of developing special endurance," so development "depends on the optimal selection of the relative volumes of work of different intensity and duration"; and "Endurance training causes more profound changes than explosive training within the body and requires more time for restoration," which pushes toward concurrent means "which may not always be appropriate for highly qualified athletes (Platonov, 1980)" (PDF p. 373 / printed p. 362, checked against the page image). They then describe "two opposing viewpoints" and a third (same page):
1. **Concurrent.** "concurrent development of general and special endurance" (Matveyev 1970; Ogoltsov 1971; Nabatnikova 1972), introducing "special endurance loading right from the beginning of the preparatory period." Corroborated "with athletes who had not yet reached the highest levels of sports mastery," namely junior middle-distance runners (Baranov 1969), swimmers (Kuzovenkov 1969) and skiers (Malikov 1974).
2. **Sequential.** "one begins by enhancing cardiovascular capability, followed by anaerobic-glycolytic endurance, and finally, short-term endurance (the creatine phosphate process)." "The introduction of aerobic work in this sequence promotes the training-effect of anaerobic work" (Ozolin 1959, 1970; Volkov 1963; Yakovlev 1957; Borisov 1979; Loktev 1978). "When one's cardiovascular ability is insufficient, an excessive increase in the volume of anaerobic means causes a decrease in sporting performance" (Naumenko 1978; Vavilov 1977; Serafimova 1974; Morzhevikov 1980).
3. **Third viewpoint.** "the increase in volume of concurrent aerobic and anaerobic training means, but with a sequential change in emphasis from general to special endurance," shown effective "for highly qualified middle-distance runners (Doroshchenko, 1976; Loktev, 1978; Borisov, 1979), as well as for multi-year training (Linyets, 1979)." The authors hedge: "One can assume that this system represents a compromise which combines the benefits of concurrent and sequential special endurance training."

**Why it works** — For viewpoint 2 the authors give a mechanism: "A gradual increase in the duration of cardiovascular loading leads to an accumulation of energy substrates and an increase in the body's energy potential (Yakovlev, et al, 1960)," and "Here, the intensity of loading, rather than its volume is of principal significance (Astrand & Rodahl, 1970)" (PDF p. 373). For viewpoints 1 and 3 they give the planners' assumptions, not mechanisms.

**When to apply** — Choosing how to order general and special endurance across a preparatory period. Inference: by the populations named, viewpoint 1 is the documented choice for athletes below the top level, and viewpoint 3 for highly qualified middle-distance runners; viewpoint 2 carries the warning about adding anaerobic volume before the aerobic base is adequate. Eric's baseline: aerobic work is kept "below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 124, Explicit). Eric's baseline: glycolytic conditioning is programmed "in the off-season" (line 117, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)). Inference: placing that glycolytic work after an aerobic base fits viewpoint 2's warning.

Inference: for football, where the energy-system priorities differ from middle-distance running (baseline line 116), these models are background, not a template.

**Example** — The authors' own population for viewpoint 3: highly qualified middle-distance runners whose aerobic and anaerobic volume rose together while the emphasis shifted from general to special endurance over the annual cycle (Doroshchenko 1976; Loktev 1978; Borisov 1979; PDF p. 373). # How Long One Emphasis Keeps Paying: Explosive Strength Plateaus in 3-4 Months, Aerobic Fitness in 2-3, Glycolytic Capacity Peaks at About 4

**What it is** — The authors say the duration of a load "can easily be miscalculated by the average coach," and that besides the overall limit set by the body's current adaptation reserves, "there is also an upper limit to the duration of using any specialised training means with a primary emphasis, the exceeding of which is detrimental to the development of maximum and explosive strength, as well as to the growth of aerobic and anaerobic capacity. Exceeding this limit does not enhance fitness and wastes the athlete's time and energy" (PDF p. 370 / printed p. 359, checked against the page image). They admit "there is no special research directed at determining the optimal length of time," and offer "indirect data" (same page):
- **Absolute strength.** A "linear increase ... which slows down as the limit of this optimal time-span of training is reached"; yet in highly qualified athletes "absolute strength increases with little variation, rising continuously during the year's training."
- **Explosive strength.** "the sharper its growth, the earlier it plateaus. When one is emphasizing the development of explosive strength exclusively, the plateau appears within 3-4 months." Where it "is not the key ability (e.g. in a mono-cycle of periodisation in the annual training of decathletes)," it "can continue (with some fluctuation) for up to 10 months."
- **Aerobic.** "significant increases in aerobic efficiency even within one month" (Borisov 1979; Sirenko 1980). Aerobic fitness and aerobic-zone loading "(at a HR of 120-170 beats/minute)" rise together, "linear over a 2-3 months period"; after that, "Despite increased loading volume, the aerobic fitness indicators do not increase significantly ... but fluctuate around the maximum level achieved" (five citations, Zatsiorsky et al 1974 to Sirenko 1980).
- **Anaerobic-glycolytic.** "About 4 months are necessary to achieve the highest results in anaerobic-glycolytic productivity" (four citations). Then: "Increasing the volume of anaerobic work produces a positive effect only if it precedes a significant volume of aerobic work, thereby stimulating the aerobic reaction (Serafimova, 1974; Naumenko, 1978)."

The scope note: the figures apply to "the natural conditions of an athlete's preparation," with other tasks trained alongside, match the volumes "highly qualified athletes use," and are "not definitive. However, they offer a preliminary guide" (PDF p. 370).

**Why it works** — The authors tie the slowing of gains to "exhaustion of the body's current adaptation energy (see 1.16)" (PDF p. 370). No further mechanism is given per quality.

**When to apply** — Setting the length of a stage that emphasises one quality, and deciding when a plateau means "change the stimulus" rather than "add volume." Inference: an aerobic emphasis that has run 2-3 months without further gain is, by these figures, at its ceiling for now, and more volume is not the lever. Eric's baseline: "Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 59, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: these time limits give a rough expectation of when a plateau is due.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors call the data indirect and the durations provisional. **Unclear wording:** the anaerobic sentence says anaerobic volume helps "only if it precedes a significant volume of aerobic work" (PDF p. 370), but on PDF p. 373 the sequential model puts aerobic first ("The introduction of aerobic work in this sequence promotes the training-effect of anaerobic work") and on PDF p. 372 "glycolytic-anaerobic exercises follow large volumes of aerobic work" is listed as a negative interaction. Inference: the p. 370 sentence may mean "is preceded by," which would fit p. 373 but not the session-level warning on p. 372; the book does not resolve it. These are times to plateau under one emphasis; they are not residual (detraining) durations, which Issurin gives separately ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]). Inference: the plateau figures come largely from track-and-field and endurance athletes; for football, where qualities are trained together, the decathlete case (explosive strength rising for up to 10 months when it is not the sole aim) may be the closer analogue.

**Example** — The authors' own contrast: explosive strength trained exclusively plateaus within 3-4 months, while in decathletes on a mono-cycle, where it is one quality among many, it can keep rising for up to 10 months (PDF p. 370 / printed p. 359).

# Volume Drives Long-Term Adaptation and Prepares Connective Tissue; Intensify Only After Extensive Low-Intensity Work

**What it is** — The authors give volume two roles. First: "The function of the volume of the load consists chiefly of the systematic and prolonged disturbance of the body's homeostasis, which stimulates the mobilisation of its energy resources and plastic reserves. This is the fundamental condition for switching from the acute (specific) reaction ... to the general (non-specific) adaptive reaction, and then to the development of long-term adaptation of the body. Therefore, in each successive annual cycle athletes should execute larger volumes of loading (within optimal limits) to raise and maintain the special work-capacity" (PDF p. 369 / printed p. 358, checked against the page image). Second, in sports with "brief, highly concentrated efforts": "the mechanical integrity of the ligamentous-joint apparatus can become the limiting factor to the progress of sporting performance" (italics in the original). "If these connective tissues are not prepared by extensive work of moderate intensity, then the great dynamic overloading encountered at the level of peak performance can lead to severe joint injury. This occurs frequently in gymnastics, weightlifting, high jumping and triple jumping" (same page).

Volume alone is not enough: "the influence of the volume can be determined correctly only if one also takes into consideration the magnitude of the loading, its duration and intensity" (PDF p. 369). Magnitude is set "first of all, on the basis of the athlete's qualification": the higher the qualification, the larger the yearly and stage volume, and the share of "specialised loading" grows (Panov 1975; Zhikharevich 1976; Vankov 1977; Matveyev 1977; Gilyazova 1978). The annual volume is "established individually" from the preceding stages; "A more serious task" is the optimal volume per month, stage or phase (same page). On intensity: it "determines the strength and specificity of its effect on the body," regulates "the training potential of the given means," frequency and intervals, and "the ratio of the volume of the loading divided by the time taken to reach the maximum load in a given stage," a measure of "loading concentration relative to time." "Intensification of loading is permitted during specific stages in the annual cycle and only after preliminary preparation with extensive low intensity loading (see Fig 6.1)" (PDF p. 370 / printed p. 359, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is the one quoted: prolonged homeostatic disturbance mobilises "energy resources and plastic reserves" and moves the body from an acute to a general, then long-term, adaptive reaction (PDF p. 369). For connective tissue they refer back to 1.6 and 1.7.2 and give no further mechanism here.

**When to apply** — Building a multi-year plan (raise annual volume, within limits, as qualification rises) and opening each year with extensive moderate-intensity work before intensifying, especially in jumping and other high-impact events. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill ...)" (line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors' "extensive low intensity loading" before intensification is close to the work-capacity base of that hierarchy.

**When NOT to apply** — "within optimal limits" is not quantified, and the rule to raise volume every year cannot run indefinitely; the authors elsewhere set a limit by current adaptation reserves (PDF p. 370) and an optimum above which the LDTE pattern appears (PDF p. 374, [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]). The joint-injury link is stated as frequent in four sports with no data. Inference: in American collegiate football, where many athletes are four- or five-year players, a rising-volume rule would need to be weighed against Eric's baseline that recovery is handled "through training-load design alone" (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)), since nothing else would catch an overshoot. The book's 4.1.2 passage gives volume two different functions (a functional base and endurance development; [[heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination]]); Inference: the two lists overlap on the "base" role and differ on the second, so read them together rather than as rival definitions.

**Example** — The authors' own: gymnastics, weightlifting, high jumping and triple jumping, where joint injury "occurs frequently" if connective tissue has not been prepared by extensive moderate-intensity work before peak dynamic loads (PDF p. 369 / printed p. 358). Inference: a jumper's year would open with weeks of moderate-volume, lower-impact jumping and strength work before depth jumps.
